maintopic: STATEMENT ON DELIVERY AND QUOTA POSITION

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. Jack McIntosh (Swift Current-Maple
Creek): Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. On Wednesday last, July 27, the minister was asked several questions with regard to the quota system as it pertains to grain producers in the prairie provinces. In reply to my question as to whether the 128 points still on the 6-bushel quota were the same points that were on low quotas in previous years, the minister stated he would have the answer later this week. I wonder if the minister is now in a position to advise the house about this situation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: STATEMENT ON DELIVERY AND QUOTA POSITION
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. On Monday I reported that there were 128 points still on the 6-bushel quota. That number has now been reduced to 52, so that most of the stations are now on the 7-bushel quota.
With regard to the specific question, a year ago, on July 31, 1959 there were 183 stations on the 6-bushel delivery quota. I took this up with the Canadian wheat board in August and asked them to give special consideration to those stations during the course of the present crop year. That has been done. I checked with the wheat board on several occasions during the course of the year to make sure that those stations which had complained about being on a low quota for several years would be given special attention. They were on a low quota because of conditions during the course of this crop year and the previous crop year, when a certain amount of grain in the northern part of the three prairie provinces was damp and had to be moved rather quickly to the terminal elevators.
During the early part of this year I mentioned that fact on several occasions. I think the farmers generally in western Canada appreciated the fact that in order that the damp grain might be moved rapidly some would have to wait their turn on the quota. Nevertheless the 183 stations that were checked last year are all on the 7-bushel quota and were on the 7-bushel quota on July

27 when the question was asked. The wheat board has met the necessary requirement there.
The board informs me that the space situation at these points is such that the delivery of the full 7-bushel quota should be possible by July 31. If at the end of the crop year there are some stations still on the 6-bushel quota, or some on the 7-bushel quota where deliveries have been inadequate due to full storage space, I will do the same thing again with the wheat board and check to make sure that during the course of the next crop year those stations receive special attention.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON DELIVERY AND QUOTA POSITION
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. Can the minister tell us the area in which the 52 stations still on the 6-bushel quota are located? Is it in the southern part of the province or the northern part?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: STATEMENT ON DELIVERY AND QUOTA POSITION
speechtext: I do not have the actual area and cannot say whether it is in the north or south, but perhaps I could give a rundown of the quota distribution. Of the 2,007 stations, in Ontario there are 2 on the 7-bushel quota; in Manitoba 369, or the entire group; in Saskatchewan 11 on the 6-bushel quota and 1,071 on 7; in Alberta 41 on the 6-bushel quota and 508 on 7, and in British Columbia 5 stations all told on the 7-bushel quota. The grand total is 52 still on 6-bushels and 1,955 on 7. I will find out for the hon. member what areas are affected by the 11 in Saskatchewan and 41 in Alberta.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON DELIVERY AND QUOTA POSITION
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. In addition to the welcome announcement about special attention next year, I wonder whether the minister has given any consideration to whether deliveries could take place for a short time within the new crop year, perhaps for two weeks, so the 7-bushel quota could in fact be available to producers at all points.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: STATEMENT ON DELIVERY AND QUOTA POSITION
speechtext:
I dealt with that question the other day, but it might be worth while to expand it a bit. I discussed with the wheat board the general subject of extension of quotas beyond July 31. As hon. members know, the initial quotas for the 1960-61 crop year become effective on August 1. This is in accordance with the practice of the wheat board, and the same policy has been followed over the last few years. In the opinion of the wheat board it is better to end each year's delivery quota on July 31 and open up with initial delivery quotas for the ensuing crop year on August 1. If delivery quotas were extended for a period after July 31, all deliveries would have to be for the account of the 1960-1961 pool, because under the terms of the Canadian Wheat Board Act
Inquiries of the Ministry July 31 is the terminal date for all pools. The extension of old quotas into a new crop year would result in delaying deliveries under new quotas which become effective on August 1.
Nevertheless, as I mentioned the other day, in one or two instances where box cars arrive on the last day of the crop year I think the practice has been to see that those box cars are filled up, even if it is August 1, and sent on their way. Generally speaking, however, the quotas and the deliveries end on July 31 for the 1959-60 crop year, and the new crop year opens on August 1.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING ARREST OF CERTAIN CHINESE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING ARREST OF CERTAIN CHINESE
speechtext:
While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house that I am advised that reports which have appeared in the press regarding the arrest of two Chinese in Montreal yesterday are inaccurate, especially in so far as mention was made that these Chinese were arraigned as much as three hours after their arrest. In fact I am advised that they were arrested at 1 p.m. and were before the court at 2.30 p.m.
In view of the adverse reaction and in some respects unjustifiable criticism with respect to the questioning that has been carried on in the past, may I say there has been no questioning at all of these two persons, on this occasion at least. Upon arrest they were taken directly to the R.C.M.P. headquarters for fingerprinting only and then taken directly before a judge. They have been released on bail. Further arrests are expected within a few days.
On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. Is the minister in a position to report on the investigation being conducted by the R.C.M.P. into the alleged perjury in the Eccles divorce case heard before the miscellaneous private bills committee this year? speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member's question anticipates something which has not yet commenced, that is, an investigation by the R.C.M.P. A day or two ago I received a letter from the chief of the committees branch transmitting to me the report of the committee, and I also received a day or two ago the transcript of the evidence. In considering this matter I have felt that inasmuch as the matters concern themselves with two possible species of misconduct, first collusion and second perjury, and inasmuch as either or both of these, if they occurred, occurred also and
(Mr. Fulton.]
primarily with respect to the proceedings before the Senate committee, it would be only appropriate that I should communicate with the chairman of the Senate committee to see whether that hon. senator or his committee felt that there was further action their committee desired to take in the matter. I have indicated to him and I am ready to refer the question to the attorney general of Ontario, especially with regard to perjury, but I believe also the attorney general of Quebec should be informed in that regard. I felt it would not be proper for me to do so without obtaining the comments of the Senate committee first.
Of course, with respect to the matter of collusion, if there be collusion, that would have been committed or would have resulted in an abuse of the procedures of parliament but primarily in the Senate committee itself, and it is of course within the power of that body to deal with such an offence, if such an offence were committed in connection with the hearings there.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very appreciative of the privilege of moving, on behalf of the right hon. the Prime Minister, the motion which stands in his name on the order paper. The motion, as hon. members will appreciate, asks that the house rescind the resolution adopted by this house on June 14 and substitute therefor a new resolution. The new resolution is in exactly the same form as the original resolution, with the exception that it omits reference to county and district court judges.
The effect of the new resolution therefore, Mr. Speaker, will be to ask Her Majesty to place before the United Kingdom parliament a proposal to amend the British North America Act to provide a retirement age of 75 for the judges of the superior courts ol the provinces of Canada. This change is made necessary-I cannot go so far as to say desirable-by the fact that the other place, in dealing with a motion they had before them which had been in identical terms to the resolution which we adopted on June 14, came to the conclusion that they should delete the reference to district and county court judges.

B.N.A. Act
The situation then was that we were faced with the necessity of taking action to deal with our own resolution in order to avoid the possibility of Her Majesty being confronted with humble addresses from the two different houses of the parliament of Canada in two different forms. This, it seemed to us, was a most undesirable if not an improper position for us to contemplate the crown being placed in. While therefore, Mr. Speaker, the government felt that its own view as to the form of the resolution was correct, nevertheless we came to the conclusion also that the exigencies of the situation, in all their implications, indicated that the preferable course was for us to invite this house to rescind its own resolution and adopt a new one which would be in exact conformity with the resolution of the Senate.
This having been done-and I trust this house will agree that this is the preferable course-then the two addresses founded on the resolution may be forwarded, and will be in identical terms. This is, of course, I am satisfied, what parliament would wish to see when we present addresses of this far-reaching importance and consequence to Her Majesty.
I have said that we felt this was the preferable course, and I should perhaps add we felt it was a course that could be adopted with propriety under the circumstances, notwithstanding our previous expression of opinion that it was desirable to include the reference to district and county court judges. In arriving at our conclusion that this was the preferable course, we were reinforced by the realization that in asking the House of Commons to adopt this course we would be achieving the major purpose which we presented to the house, that is of insuring that there will be a retiring age limit of 75 for superior court judges. We realized also that the determination of the retiring age of county court judges might then still be made in accordance with the present provisions of the Judges Act. In adopting this course we are achieving the major purpose, and we are not producing the result that the district and county court judges will have no retiring age limit set because their retiring age may continue to be determined, as at present, by the Judges Act.
On the basis of these considerations, but for the primary reason that we felt it would be undesirable that this parliament should present to Her Majesty addresses in two different forms, one from each house, we came to the conclusion that we should ask the House of Commons to rescind its resolution and substitute another.

Now, with respect to the procedure being followed, the authorities have been consulted, and I think there is no question but that this is the proper course, although it looks cumbersome on the order paper. Our position is that there is authority to the effect that the resolution can be rescinded and a new one substituted therefor, and that this is preferable to a motion to amend a resolution already adopted.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I submit to the house this new resolution calling for the rescinding of the earlier one and the adoption of the new one.

Mr. Speaker, the views of the official opposition in regard to the purpose of the resolution which is now before the house were made known when we discussed the previous resolution, and I do not need to repeat those views on this occasion. At that time we expressed our support for an amendment to the British North America Act, which was undoubtedly required to provide for a retiring age for superior court judges. There was no difference of opinion between the government and ourselves on that score, although there was a difference of opinion as to whether this provision should be made applicable, as we thought, only to judges that were to be appointed henceforth.
However, Mr. Speaker, the decision of the house on that matter was reached, and I have no desire to reopen that question. The decision has been taken. However, this resolution before us today differs from the earlier resolution, as the Minister of Justice has pointed out, in the omission of the previous provision for an amendment to the British North America Act covering the retirement age of district and county court judges.
That provision is omitted. That was a provision that we did our best to have taken out, for reasons which we indicated at some length at the time the earlier resolution was before the house. We were not successful. The other house, however, decided that this provision should be omitted and it saves parliament, as the minister has put it-and indeed the British parliament-from the embarrassment of attempting to deal with two resolutions, not identical, in connection with an amendment to the constitution, the government has decided to accept this omission as recommended by the other house and has submitted this new resolution which implements that decision.
I think the government has been extremely wise in taking this course, which in our view saves this parliament from the consequences of a reversion to colonialism-

It will be a simple matter to show that. At a time when the Prime Minister has called for a conference or rather has accepted an invitation to a conference which would repatriate, so we hope, the rest of our constitution; while that initiative was being taken, a step had been taken in this house which, if it had been carried out, would have resulted in the expatriation of a part of the constitution which is now under our control.
There has been a good deal of public misunderstanding of the meaning of this provision as it appeared in the first resolution, and some misinterpretation of the effect of its removal. As the minister himself has pointed out, this provision has nothing whatever to do with the retiring age of county court or district court judges. It has nothing whatever to do with that matter. The federal government has legislated for that purpose now without challenge, so far as I know, for 73 years. Under that legislation of this parliament the present age limit of 75 years for district and county court judges was established, I believe, as far back as 1913.
There is therefore no question of re-establishing a retirement age which was established so many years ago. All that this provision would have done-I refer to the one which is now omitted-was to have removed, according to the minister, doubts about the constitutionality of those actions which have been taken by this parliament over a period of 73 years without challenge. When we discussed this matter previously, I referred on June 14 to a question on this specific point. It was a question asked in the session of 1927, and it will be found at page 1080 of Hansard of that year. It was a question asked by the then hon. member for Sim-coe, Mr. Boys, of the minister of justice of that day. The question was this:
Is there any special provision in the British North America Act with respect to the retirement of county court judges?
The then minister of justice said no. Another question was asked:
Is it suggested that such legislation was ultra vires?
The reply given was:
No, not at all. .. There is nothing in the British North America Act preventing us from dealing with the tenure of office of county court judges.
However, when we discussed this matter previously the Minister of Justice said that while the provision has not been challenged in the courts there is involved, as he put it at page 4907 of Hansard, a residual doubt. Indeed, in his communications with the provinces on this matter he said there was a serious doubt.
B.N.A. Act
As a result, we were asked in this house to resolve this doubt which, so far as I know, had not been in anybody's mind previously; at least there had been no public expression of that doubt, so far as I am aware. We were asked to resolve this doubt not by carrying on until our constitution was entirely repatriated, at which time we could resolve it in our own way if there was any doubt; we were asked to resolve it not by submitting the question to our own supreme court for a decision. No; after the expiration of 73 years we were asked to resolve this so-called residual doubt or serious doubt by asking the parliament of the United Kingdom to declare that we were wrong, that we in this parliament did not in fact have this power which we had been exercising for 73 years, and therefore to ask the parliament of the United Kingdom if it would please amend our constitution and make us honest Canadians again.
That request, Mr. Speaker, was made by a government which talks a good deal about Canadian nationalism and Canadian national development. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what would have been the reaction in the British House of Commons or in the British parliament upon receiving from this great independent state of Canada a request of this kind, to change our constitution in respect of something over which we have had control for 73 years.
That was the only issue involved in this particular provision which appeared in the earlier resolution, Mr. Speaker, and even at this stage I am glad the government has decided not to take the course which it advocated should be taken a few weeks ago, and which at that time we tried to persuade it not to take.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a brief word on this subject. The Minister of Justice will remember that when the matter was before the house, I did state my views with regard to this situation. The minister and I had several exchanges as he will recall. The Leader of the Opposition in his succinct statement has made a comprehensive coverage of the problem in so far as this party is concerned, but I believe there is a situation arising out of the position of the government at the present time that must not be overlooked.
The minister has been preoccupied during the past ten days with consultations with the government of the United States in Washington, with his responsibilities as spokeman for the government on the combines act, and with heavy obligations as spokesman for the government in the bill of rights committee. I can only in all charity attribute this heavy preoccupation as the reason for the position in which the minister now finds himself. Other members of the government may not have as valid an excuse, but in the light of what I am going to say I recognize that that is the case so far as the Minister of Justice is concerned. But the Minister of Justice is the spokesman for the government of Canada in this House of Commons. He is not as other private members are. He has a responsibility not only as a member of this house but also as a member of the government.
Mr. Speaker, what was the position of the government regarding this matter when it was first discussed in this house? The position, as the Leader of the Opposition has stated, was that in the matter of the tenure of office of the county and district court judges, the minister felt there was a doubt as to the authority of this parliament to deal

with this question in any way notwithstanding the fact, as was pointed out, that from 1867 and more particularly from 1873 on this parliament had take measures directly in relation to the tenure of office of district and county court judges.
We argued that to ask the United Kingdom parliament for leave to amend our constitution so as to give parliament the power to deal with the tenure of office of district and county court judges was to ask the United Kingdom parliament to do something which we now have the power ourselves to discharge. As the Leader of the Opposition said, to take that course now would be a retrogressive step and that would be going back to the colonial period so far as Canada was concerned. We argued that was objectionable particularly at a time when through one of our provinces, the province of Quebec, initiative was being taken in the matter of acquiring for Canada the right to amend our constitution without resort to any legislative body outside Canada.
Surely the Minister of Justice owes the house a fuller explanation than he has given. We recognize that as a result of the action taken in the other place, the situation now is that Her Majesty's government in the United Kingdom would be confronted with two resolutions from the houses of this parliament which, in part, are in conflict with one another. To allow that situation would be a reflection, as the Leader of the Opposition has said, on the responsible independent position that must be taken by a parliament such as the parliament of Canada.
What the Minister of Justice has not explained is this. Does he now say that the action we took in this house prior to the passage of the resolution with regard to county and district court judges was a valid position to take? Is he now satisfied beyond doubt that this parliament has the right to deal with the tenure of county and district court judges without resort to an amendment of the constitution by the parliament of the United Kingdom? The minister must be in that position before he can accede to the suggested way out of the dilemma in which he has been placed.
The minister cannot accept this solution merely on the grounds of expediency or merely to relieve the government of an embarrassment; he cannot accept it because he is faced with the dying days of this session and that accordingly this is the best way out of the muddle caused by the government's failure to appreciate the constitutional position regarding the tenure of county and district court judges. That, surely, is the
B.N.A. Act
situation. The government cannot agree to a course such as this on the mere ground of expediency. It must be backed up by conviction and by an appreciation of what the true constitutional position is. If the minister will now tell the house that it is the considered opinion of himself, of the law officers of the crown and of the government, that the position he took in this house prior to the vote on the resolution has now been changed as a result of further consideration, then of course he will extricate himself from the difficulty in which he now finds himself.
What were the grounds for saying that we must go to the parliament of the United Kingdom to obtain the necessary power to deal with the tenure of office of district and county court judges? What were the grounds presented by the minister? We pointed out the precedents. We pointed out what was done in 1873 and we pointed out what happened in 1926 when the then minister of justice, Mr. Lapointe, in answer to a question asked by Mr. Boys in the presence of such outstanding legal luminaries as the late Lord Bennett and Mr. Cahan, said there was no doubt about the constitutional right of this parliament to deal with matters having to do with the tenure of office of district and county court judges. The Minister of Justice heard that argument prior to the vote in this house on the resolution. He did not agree with that position. He said there was some doubt about the situation, although I think the only evidence of doubt was an observation made by the attorney general of, I believe, the province of Saskatchewan. The minister apparently agreed with that doubt. Does he still agree with it?
The important thing is whether the minister now believes that it is not necessary to go to the parliament of the United Kingdom to get the necessary authority to deal with the tenure of office of county and district court judges. Unless the minister can answer that question in the affirmative, he is now taking, in my judgment, pursuant to the high responsibilities of a minister of justice, an irresponsible course. The minister cannot act merely on the ground of expediency. He cannot act merely because he wishes to extricate himself from the difficulty which the circumstances present.
We in this party believe that it is desirable to retire judges at the age of 75. We have taken the position that in order to provide for the compulsory retirement of superior court judges, authority must now come from the United Kingdom parliament. We have always taken the position that authority of this kind was not required in connection with the

B.N.A. Act
tenure of district and county court judges. But having taken that position, we are now faced with a situation which confirms our fears and our concern. The position taken by the minister prior to the passage of the resolution has been repudiated, not only by a decision in the other place but by the very act which the government now accepts.
Surely the government owes the house a much more careful explanation than the minister has so far given us. The minister must now tell us, "I was wrong". The position, he must now agree, is clearly that this parliament has the right to deal with the tenure of county and district court judges. If the minister takes that position we shall respect him for it. But if not, I say that the course taken by the hon. gentleman is not a responsible one.

I wish to rise briefly to reinforce what has been said by my hon. friend from Essex East, and to reinforce it out of the mouth, in part, of the Minister of Justice himself, because it does seem to me that the point raised by the hon. member for Essex East deserves a serious answer.
I say this with all the more conviction because when I made the same argument in the debate on June 14, as had previously been made by the Leader of the Opposition on this point, the argument that this was a reversion to colonialism and that it was totally unnecessary because the jurisdiction of this parliament had never been questioned, my contentions were ridiculed. I pointed out that no question had been raised regarding this jurisdiction by anyone of eminence in this country since county court judges were retired at the age of 75 in 1913; indeed since Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, who later became chief justice of Canada, had asked parliament to provide for the retirement of judges at 80 years of age in 1903; since Mr. Doherty had done the same thing in 1913, changing the age to 75; since Mr. Lapointe in 1926 took the position to which my hon. friend from Essex East referred, in reply to a Conservative member of that day. I said it was an extraordinary thing that the present Minister of Justice or the Prime Minister should suddenly have had a revelation that every government and every parliament up to this day had been wrong and they were right.
When I made that argument following the Leader of the Opposition, who had already made it one June 14, it was ridiculed. I should therefore like to repeat a few of the words
I Mr. Martin (Essex East).]
I used on that occasion. I will not go over most of what I said, but I did use these words:
However, if they feel there is a doubt-
That is the government. I continue:
-I hope they will refer the matter to the courts. Surely it is the height of colonialism-and no other word can be applied to it-to seek to vest in Westminster a jurisdiction which they have never had-* which they did not assume in 1867 and of which certainly, once the Statute of Westminster was passed, they divested themselves-and to seek to put into a British statute something no one has ever questioned since 1867 until the minister had this bright idea quite recently, namely the right of this parliament to do something which this parliament has done over and over again and which has been the basis of the tenure of county and district court judges since the year 1913 without any kind of question. It almost passes comprehension why a government should seek to be so abject.
The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) interjected at this point, "Nonsense". I went on to say:
What purpose they think this is going to serve it is very hard to perceive.
The hon. member for Carleton again interjected:

It was not the case of an address being adopted here and forwarded to the Senate for their concurrence. Identical addresses were submitted in each chamber. We adopted our address without change. Each one of them has said that the exclusive right of the parliament of Canada to legislate with respect to the tenure of office of district and county court judges has ben accepted without challenge for 73 years. That is not the case, Mr. Speaker, and that statement reveals the lack of preparation and consideration given to this matter by hon. members who used those words.
The fact is that there have been circumstances giving rise to doubt as to where the authority to legislate with respect to the tenure of office of district and county court judges resides ever since 1869, when the legislature of Ontario enacted a statute dealing with the tenure of office of district and county court judges. That statute continued in existence on the statute books of the province of Ontario until the year 1953, I think it was, when it was finally removed in the course of one of their annual revisions. Hence to say that there has been no doubt about this matter for 73 years is as complete a misstatement as are most of the other statements that have been made about the matter by the members of the opposition in the course of this debate.

Apparently hon. members opposite cannot agree among themselves as to the length of time for which it has been without challenge.
However, my main point is that it has not been without challenge, and that that challenge has continued ever since 1869, when the legislature of Ontario passed a statute dealing with the tenure of office of district and county court judges, which came immediately under question by the minister of justice of Canada, who at that time was Sir John A. Macdonald. Sir John A. Macdonald took the position that the statute as originally passed in the legislature of Ontario was open to great question.
There is a long history of discussion of that matter which is reflected in the Journals, I think it is, of this house. These record the correspondence which took place between the government here and representatives or officials of the government of Ontario. From reading the original correspondence it appears that the time for disallowance had gone by on the first occasion when it could have been exercised. So there was correspondence between officials of the two governments, and the Ontario government agreed to submit to its legislature another bill amending its original bill.
However, the subsequent statute also dealt, although in an amended form, with the matter of the tenure of office of district and county court judges in Ontario, and it is quite obvious from the correspondence and the discussion which took place with respect to the legislation that there was a very fundamental difference of opinion as to whether the parliament of Canada had the exclusive right to legislate with respect to the tenure of office of county or district court judges.
I might refer hon. members, if they want to follow up the interest which 1 am sure they have in this matter, to an article appearing in the Canadian Law Journal of 1881, volume 17, starting at page 445, in which the author of the article took the position that although the matter had been brought under question, that the authority lay with the parliament of Canada. The editor of the law journal appended an editorial note at the end of the article in which he reviewed some

B.N.A. Act
of the authorities and some of the considerations relative to this question.
The position of the government, therefore, with respect to this matter has been that it could not be asserted that there is no question as to where the legislative authority resides and that our constitution is not absolutely clear on the point. There is one other view which I think deserves mention; that because of the silence of the British North America Act on the point, the authority to determine the question of the tenure of office of district and county court judges lies perhaps not so much with the parliament of Canada as with the Governor General.
I think probably the best view is that the complete authority over this question does reside somewhere in the federal field, but that whether it be with the Governor General or with the parliament of Canada itself is a question; and there has been a very considerable and authoritative body of opinion which holds that it is open to question as to whether it lies between the federal and provincial authorities.
So, Mr. Speaker, in the light of that brief resume of the differences of opinion which have been expressed, differences of opinion which, as I say, resulted in a legislative enactment by the legislature of Ontario which continued on their statute books until 1953, I think it is desirable to resolve the doubts and to resolve them in a manner which would place the matter beyond any question.
In asking the house to consider the reasonableness of that point of view, I think I should remind the house that this suggestion of a constitutional amendment which is now before the house is the first time since confederation that we have asked that the British North America Act be amended with respect to the tenure of office of judges. This is the first time since 1867 that the parliament of Canada has asked the United Kingdom parliament to amend the British North America Act in that respect.
There is no doubt that with respect to the tenure of office of superior court judges the only way in which it is proper to ask for an amendment is first to obtain provincial consent and then to ask the United Kingdom parliament to make that amendment in the British North America Act. That is agreed to by every hon. member of the house who has spoken in this debate.

Second, he has misinterpreted what he himself said I said. I said there was some opinion which held that although it may be agreed that authority in this matter lies in the federal field, yet, because of the silence of the British North America Act on the question of the tenure and removal from office of county court judges authority in this matter rests with the Governor General. I did not say it rests with the Governor General. I said there was argument that that might be the case, and I refer the hon. gentleman to the remarks of Lord Watson in the case of the Attorney General for Canada v. the attorney general for Ontario (1898) Appeal Cases, 247.
That was not my decision. A Conservative government was not in office at that time; a Liberal government was in office.
What I say is that there is doubt about the matter for the reasons I have given; reasons which, I submit, would lead the average reasonable person to a conclusion that there is indeed some doubt about it. So I said, this being the situation, it seemed to us proper that when we for the first time submit an

address to ask that the British North America Act be amended to deal with the tenure of office of judges, we should take the opportunity at the same time to ask that the authority to deal with the tenure of district and county court judges should also be placed beyond doubt, and that it should be placed beyond doubt within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada.
There is nothing whatever of colonialism in that position. It is a reasonable, logical and proper position to take. It is a position which asserts the pre-eminence of Canada in this field, and which attempts to have the situation resolved in the only way in which I submit it can be resolved at this time, that is by a constitutional enactment.
If there is any responsibility for the fact that at the present time we still have to go to the United Kingdom parliament in order to get this sort of constitutional amendment, the responsibility certainly does not rest with the present government of Canada. Indeed, the present government of Canada has given notice in unmistakable terms of its intention to attempt to resolve this problem and produce a method by which authority to amend the constitution of Canada may be brought home to Canada. That was announced by the Prime Minister in the course of his remarks this session, when he was speaking in the debate on the address. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I, together with those who sit on this side of the house, have listened with interest to the remarks made by the Minister of Labour concerning his department during the course of his opening statement. While his statement was an interesting one, I think all of us will agree it was a statement which had to do with the activities of his department. Important as those activities are, in my opinion very little was said during the course of his remarks concerning the very important problem with which this country is faced at the present

time. Of course, I refer to the serious economic problem of unemployment. The minister, while he spoke for some 30 minutes or more, did not give to the committee a detailed statement other than what had been said by the Prime Minister and his other colleague concerning a frontal attack upon the problem which faces us today.
What is the problem? Earlier during this year, when the matter was under discussion in the house, and I refer now to February, 1960, there were 800,000 Canadians out of work and seeking employment. This represented 8.1 per cent of the labour force of this country. The Toronto Star, dealing with that question in its weekly editorial on February 27, 1960, had this to say:
As parliament and various provincial legislatures opened this year, speeches from the throne glowed with confidence about the return of good times and of surging economic activity in 1960. At the very same time 723,000 Canadians were looking for jobs through national employment service. Not all, but the great majority of these were out of work.
The two views do not jibe. There may be good times, but not for the hundreds of thousands of people-and their families-having to depend on unemployment insurance instead of pay envelopes. The insurance, though a help, is no substitute for a job.
Then there is this remarkable paragraph which I should like to put on the record.
Apart from extending unemployment insurance benefits, the government's main attempts at treatment^ are to solicit the public to hire people for odd jobs ("Do it now" campaigns) and the winter works program. This program provides relatively few jobs and is certainly no answer to the problem.
At that time there was a great deal of advertising about what was known as the "Do it now" campaign. To what extent this has assisted in providing jobs for people, little or nothing has been said.
What is the position now? The hon. member for Essex East the other day put on the record the situation, and I shall not repeat it except to make one general statement. In June of this year, having regard to the latest figures from the minister's office and the dominion bureau of statistics, there were
300,000	people out of jobs and seeking work. According to the labour force survey of the dominion bureau of statistics for the month of June of this year, this represented 4.6 per cent of the labour force, unemployed and out of work. Three hundred thousand people out of work in the month of June, at a time when normally there is no seasonal unemployment and at a time when the business cycle should be at its peak, is symptomatic of a problem which, it seems to me, demands the immediate attention of the minister and all those who sit with him on the treasury
Supply-Labour
benches. Three hundred thousand people out of work at this time of the year is a serious matter.
What will the position be as time goes on? If the committee will bear with me, I shall attempt to deal with that. I hear from my left the statement, "doom and gloom". Yes, we were accused of being the prophets of doom and gloom, not only during the course of this debate but during an earlier debate, at which time the minister lost his temper and said to those of us who sit on this side of the house, what have you got to offer? Have you anything to offer? The government faced up to it with the winter works program which provided about
40,000	to 50,000 jobs, a winter works program which was announced too late in 1959 to be of any use in the province of Quebec and which was, because of the credit restrictions in 1960, of very little value. What is the solution?

Then there is the training of unemployed workers. The federal government is to increase its contribution in that field from 50 per cent to 75 per cent of the total cost. To help overcome technological unemployment we advocated the expansion of vocational training in order to develop new skills among workers. We advocated a national advisory board on economic development, automation and unemployment. We advocated a special capital fund to encourage industrial development in the Atlantic provinces. We advocated again, as we did in 1958, a national science commission to ensure the most effective use of our national resources. We urged the government to plan now against the danger of cyclical unemployment when the economic cycle turns downward again.
We must learn a lot more, we said, about seasonal unemployment than we know now. We advocated a special unemployment committee to study and analyse the problem. We must have the best brains of government, business, trade unions, agriculture and universities set to work on the study of seasonal unemployment.
I could go on but time is of the essence. What were we told from the other side of the house? In fact, these suggestions were laughed at by hon. gentlemen who sit on the side of the Minister of Labour. What did the Minister of Finance say? On March 31 the Minister of Finance said that the problem of unemployment would melt with the snow. That was in effect what the Minister of Finance told us at that time when he spoke at a meeting in Toronto. He said that with the coming of spring and with the melting of the snow the problem of unemployment also would melt and disappear.
Then again we were given some more advice by the Minister of Finance. He found a new formula which was to be added to the "Do it now" program and that was "work and save". It is an easy thing to make that statement in speeches but when it comes to putting it into operation, particularly by those who have no work, as can be seen, it is of no practical use whatsoever.
The Leader of the Opposition put on Hansard some months ago the fact that there were three kinds of unemployment, namely cyclical or economic unemployment caused by the ups and downs of business; technological unemployment caused in large part by automation; and seasonal unemployment brought about by climatic conditions. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that the government has addressed itself to only one of these categories of unemployment, namely that of a seasonal or climatic nature. The program which has been set down as a four-pronged program deals with but one of the categories.

Mr. Chairman, although this debate is taking place in the dying days of this sesion it is nevertheless an exceedingly important one. Recent statistics issued by the department show that unemployment is still a serious problem in Canada.
I have in my hands statistics of unplaced applicants as a percentage of the labour force. These show that in June this year there were 401,196 unplaced applicants. I have the figures for the same month back to 1956. In the year before this government took office, in this month, there were 191,000 unemployed in this category. In 1957, the next year, when the Conservative government had handled the administration of this country for half a year there were 270,000. In 1958 in the same month it was up to 526,000. In 1959 it was 320,000 and this year it is 401,000. Under this administration the government has been able to accomplish nothing towards reducing the general unemployment picture.
This government took office in June, 1957 and its administration since has been notable throughout for the widespread unemployment that has existed in the country. In case it might be said that the figures for June are unrepresentative, I have figures in my hand for all of the months of the same year and they show the same general trend. In January, 1957 the number of unemployed amounted to 526,000; in the same month in 1958, 816,000; in January of 1959, 775,000; and in January of this year, 772,000.
I think this is a disgrace to Canada. I do not understand why the minister in introducing his estimates did not deal with the

central problem of unemployment. Apparently the government does not think that the problem is really important. It has not attached to the problem a high priority. The government has come forward with no plan that I know of to deal with this national emergency, for that is exactly what it is.
Widespread unemployment is surely a blot on our country, not only because of the hardship to the people who are unemployed but because of the general reduction in the production of our nation and because of the great loss of material wealth. When we have widespread unemployment as we have today I would estimate that the country is losing at the very minimum $2 billion of wealth production a year. The government which has been in office for three years has seen our country forgo the production of at least $6 billion of wealth because of unemployment. That is a very high price to pay for a Tory administration which is unconcerned and certainly unable to deal with this great problem.
Not only have the minister and the government been unwilling to present a program to deal with the problem but the government has not been able to forecast that conditions are going to improve. As a matter of fact, there are a great many forecasts from officials of the departments by way of speeches that have been made which indicate that within the next year or two we may face a much deeper recession than we now have. Instead of the government coming forward with a bold program we hear rumours of the government pulling a snap election to avoid having to call an election when we are in an even deeper recession than the current one.
The Minister of Labour is in a difficult position. He has to take more of the responsibility for this situation than other members of the government because he is the minister. I do not want to be unduly harsh on the minister but the government has failed the Canadian people. It has failed to put forward a policy to solve the unemployment problem. As a matter of fact, statistics released from government departments suggest that conditions in recent days are getting worse. I have in my hand the April index of industrial production found in the D.B.S. daily bulletin of June 29 in which there is the following:
Canada's seasonally adjusted index of industrial production in April declined 2.4 per cent to 167.3 from the March level of 171.4.
An important index of economic activity in the country, the industrial index, shows a decline of 2.4 per cent. Another important

index is the gross national product, and in the D.B.S. daily bulletin for June 22 I find the following:
The advance in gross national product moderated in the first quarter of 1960. Apart from the third quarter of last year, the increase of 1 per cent was the smallest quarter to quarter gain in the value of production since the expansion began following recovery from the 1957-58 recession.
There is little indication there that we are getting out of the woods. Another economic index that is considered to be an important one in showing the buoyancy of our economy or otherwise is the index of new motor vehicle sales. Total sales of new passenger and commercial vehicles in April declined 2.7 per cent to 57,773 units from 59,360 in the corresponding month last year, while sales in the January-April period rose 1.9 per cent to 180,702 units from 177,334 a year ago. The retail value of that month's sales fell 4.2 per cent to $172 million from $179 million.
The index of motor vehicle sales indicates not only a general recession in the economy but shows the difficulty experienced in the sales of automobiles. Information is published by D.B.S. as to starts and completions of new dwellings from time to time, and the latest daily bulletin, that of June 28, states as follows:
Starts on the construction of new dwelling units in urban centres of 5,000 population and over in May fell to 6,913 from 11,151 in the same month last year, according to advance D.B.S. figures.
This is another indication of a depressed economy. Another index that is considered an important one is that showing the number of railway car loadings. The D.B.S. daily bulletin of June 30 states as follows:
Cars of railway revenue freight loaded on lines in Canada in the week ended June 21 numbered 78,867, slightly below last year's corresponding total of 79,233 cars.
Department store sales in May decreased slightly by .7 per cent to an estimated $116 million from $117 million in the corresponding 1959 month while the January to May total increased 1.7 per cent to $514 million from $505 million a year ago. The bulletin showing chain store sales indicates that chain store sales in May declined 4.3 per cent to $269 million from $281 million in the corresponding month last year.
All of these indications of economic conditions in the country show not only that we are in trouble but that conditions have been worsening. The widespread unemployment situation is having other adverse effects. When the government took office there was $852,
729,000	in the unemployment insurance fund as of June 30, 1957; after this government had been in office for a period of just 12 months, the money in the unemployment
Supply-Labour
insurance fund had dropped to $644.5 million or a loss in the first year of this administration of $208 million. After this administration had been in office a further year, the unemployment insurance fund had dropped to $434 million, a further drop of $210 million. On June 30 of this year, in spite of an increase in the amount of contributions made to the fund, the fund had dropped another $138 million to $296 million.
I should like the Minister of Labour to tell us how long, in his opinion, it is going to be until the unemployment insurance fund is bankrupt, and the government either has to borrow money or get money from the general revenues to replenish the fund or the people on unemployment will be denied benefits. The unemployment insurance fund is going into bankruptcy at a very alarming rate. Still the minister, in introducing his estimates, gave this committee and the country no hope that the government has a policy or a policy to solve unemployment, Members of this government support the present capitalist system. They like to call i1 a free enterprise system. The members ol the Liberal party support that kind of system. Whether we support the present economic order as it exists, we support our democratic processes and our free parliamentary institutions. I think the communists must be smiling in the Kremlin when they see a nation like ours, perhaps with more wealth in relation to our population than any other nation in the world, hobbling along on one leg.
This government lauds the free enterprise system. It lauds its own efforts, and yet there are half a million people unemployed while the government has no policy. I think in this day and age, when we are competing in an ideological sense with the communist world, this government should be exceedingly concerned about doing everything possible to make our economy one of full employment, full production and a high standard of living. Yet, in my opinion, the government plays into the hands of the communists by allowing our economic system to hobble along while losing $2 billion worth of production a year. In the interest of strengthening our society, in the interest of the welfare of all Canadians, I hope the government will soon come forward with a positive policy for dealing with unemployment.
There was an announcement made in the house the other day that the government was going to appoint a royal commission to inquire into the automobile industry in our country. This was a welcome announcement. I hope that action to improve the chances of employment in this industry will not have to wait the royal commission report which may

Supply-Labour
take years in its completion. Before anyone may misunderstand what I am about to say, I want to say that we in the C.C.F. party are opposed to tariffs being used as a method of combatting unemployment. We feel that the answer to unemployment in this and other industries is not to resort to the use of tariffs. There may be room for some planning, for some move toward the integration of the automobile industry of this continent.
We have in Canada automobile companies which are subsidiaries of United States parent corporations. In Canada our companies are asked, in the main, to produce exactly the same models as are produced in the United States. It would seem to me a much more sensible arrangement if in Canada our industry could produce fewer models and produce a more standard model which could be produced for the whole of North America. This kind of co-operation would remove the need for tariff protection and would bring about efficiency in the industry. I would hope it would go a long distance toward increasing employment in that industry. I only hope the government will not fold its hands and do nothing, waiting for years until the royal commission may make its report. May I say that I welcome the announcement and I hope the commission will be appointed immediately; that it can undertake its work within the next few weeks and that its report will be received at the earliest possible date.
Unemployment is a major problem in our country. As has been suggested on former occasions, this is the time for action by the government, this is the time to call a conference to consider this great national problem which should include within it representatives of provincial governments, municipalities, management and labour. It would be a conference to consider the economic welfare of the Canadian nation. This government, in this kind of conference, should not take the same attitude it took at the federal-provincial conference which just concluded. This kind of conference would require leadership. The last conference on federal-provincial fiscal relations found this government empty-handed; it went in without proposals. They said, this is just a talkfest and we will hear from the premier of each of the provinces. The suggested conference is the kind before which the government should place well defined proposals which would lead, when implemented, to the removal of unemployment in our country.
I have a number of suggestions I should like to make, Mr. Chairman. I think now is the time for a tremendous increase in investment. I should like to see a national investment board or a national investment corporation which would have available to it at least

a billion dollars to be used for investment in industries, in roads, in schools, in hospitals, in housing, in works of all kinds that would lead to a reduction in unemployment. The government takes the opposite view. The government says we are following a tight money policy; we have a high interest policy. Instead of making funds readily available, our policy has been to curtail funds in the hope that this would reduce the inflationary trend. I believe the government has to change its course completely, and that there should be available to the provinces, to municipalities and to industries, large sums of money which would enable this kind of economic expansion.
Second, I would suggest that now is the time for this government to consider special projects in its relationship with the provinces. I do not know why the government is waiting to go forward with a second trans-Canada highway. This surely is a place in which there is a need for additional services. Here is a place in which more people can be employed than we have employed at the present time. I would suggest that in addition to a second trans-Canada highway there should be an over-all road policy whereby federal money will go to assist in the construction of the main east-west and north-south roads in our country.
I would suggest that more money should be made available for hospital construction and that the Minister of Public Works should make available for house construction in this country the same funds that were made available last year. In other words, there should be no reduction in the funds for home building.
Third, I would suggest that to improve the possibility of employment in winter there may be need for special incentive, such as special tax incentive or perhaps special depreciation incentive in order to encourage industries to expand and to provide employment in the winter months.
As a fourth necessary measure to help to solve unemployment in this country I would suggest there is the whole question of a great expansion in Canadian trade. This government has tied its policy to GATT. This government has failed to use new methods in order to increase our international trade. We have a Canadian-Soviet trade agreement. There is no indication, so far as I know, that the Canadian government is going to take advantage of the fact that the soviet government has agreed to buy $2 worth of goods in our country for each $1 worth we buy in that nation. I suggest that here is a place for government planning and action. The government should take steps to buy from the Soviet union a larger quantity of

goods than we have bought in the past in order that we can expand twofold our exports to that country.
I would suggest further that now is the time for the government to consider steps to increase the incomes of Canadians, especially the incomes of Canadians whose incomes are low. If the government would bring about an increase in the old age pension from $55 to $75 a month I suggest that that injection of additional purchasing power in the hands of the elderly people in this country would be of assistance in increasing the demand for goods, thus resulting in a subsequent increase in employment.
I represent an agricultural area. The agricultural producers of Canada have often been criticized. However, there is one thing for which they have never been criticized, namely hoarding their money. If the government would do something to bolster farm income they can be assured that that income would find its way into the economy of our country and would be used to purchase farm implements, repairs, lumber and the other goods produced in our nation.
I would suggest to the Minister of Labour that he use his influence in the cabinet in order to provide an increase in the incomes of the western grain producers. I suggest that $100 million by way of deficiency payments would be an important contribution toward greater employment in our country.
They ought at least to see the farmers.

The hon. member for Essex East says that they should see the farmers. Of course they should see them. I want to congratulate the Minister of Labour for seeing the automobile workers. The automobile workers were given a hearing and they obtained a royal commission but the agricultural producers on the prairies can no longer get even so much as a hearing.
Or an answer to their letters.
We are on labour estimates, not on agriculture estimates.

This is a great economic problem facing the Canadian nation. We are in a deep economic crisis which has resulted in widespread unemployment. We in this group- those of us in the opposition-are not satisfied with a country that has at this time a half a million unemployed persons and a government that does not take the problem seriously. I suggest that before this debate is concluded the Minister of Labour should be frank with the committee and should state to the committee the proposals and the program of the government to deal with this problem.
Supply-Labour
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Will the hon. member give his reference when he spoke about the increase in retail sales?
The increase in which?
The increase in retail sales. Will the hon. member give the source of his information?

Those figures are all taken from the dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin. The figures for department store sales were taken from the D.B.S. daily bulletin of July 7 and those for chain store sales were taken from the D.B.S. daily bulletin of July 8.

May I be permitted to ask, as a supplementary question, whether the hon. gentleman is relying on the Financial Post as a substantial and reliable source of information for these figures on retail store sales?
Not at all.

I should like to endeavour to clarify several misunderstandings so that we can get down to a serious discussion of a serious problem. Time and time again I have heard comment on or reference to-in fact I have heard it ad nauseam-the Prime Minister's statement: "As long as I am Prime Minister no one will suffer from unemployment". I want to make it clear that those are the exact words he used but that he did not at any time state that there would be no unemployment if he were prime minister. Obviously the only way in which to guarantee that there would be no unemployment in any country is to reduce that country to an anthill or a slave state.
Incidentally, I should like to comment that some few weeks ago I was talking to one of the Victorian Order nurses in Cornwall who has done a magnificent job there over many years. She mentioned to me that, as is obvious, when there is unemployment there is great demoralization of the people concerned but that, nevertheless, she had noticed that there was nothing like the absolute destitution- and mind you, it was bad enough-that she had experienced in the depression when she had previously been there, although I certainly do not wish to minimize the seriousness of it or the plight of those who are without jobs.
However, I think it is perfectly obvious to any reasonable and sincere person that the Prime Minister, in saying what he was saying at that time and what he has said on several occasions, was announcing his own social and political philosophy, namely

Supply-Labour
that personal and human rights were to him far more important than property rights. I think it is because of that fact that he has done such things as raising the old age pension and extending the period of unemployment insurance benefits. On other occasions the Prime Minister has stated that just as soon as our productivity would increase sufficiently to warrant further relief to our elderly people, something would be done to relieve them. Since our productivity has increased-and the Leader of the Opposition has admitted this on more than one occasion-I feel quite convinced that something will be done before long to alleviate and assist the position of our elderly people.
The hon. member for Laurier several weeks ago in this house brought to our attention the critical unemployment situation in our respective hometown of Cornwall. I must say in all fairness that he did not exaggerate the problem which exists there and I must also thank him for his assistance although I doubt if it was given entirely on philanthropic grounds.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It was, I can assure the hon. member.

Thank you. However, he mentioned the problem in Cornwall was acute, and I believe he also mentioned the discontinuance of the seaway construction and the closing down of Canada Cottons in that area.
That is true, but there are other factors which he did not mention. He did not mention, for instance, that the textile industry, especially in that area, had been in grave difficulties for over 30 years. He did not mention that this government has done more than any other previous government to alleviate the problems of the textile industry despite the fact that its hands were tied by the previous government, by GATT and by other international arrangements. Also he did not mention that a great many people had been thrown out of work in Cornwall by the curtailment of operations on the Cornwall canal, and perhaps many of his good friends are in that category. He did not mention the difficulties of the people of Cornwall in attracting new industry to the area, despite their great initiative in forming the industrial development corporation which he mentioned to take over the property of Canadian Cottons and provide floor space to attract new industry at very advantageous rates. He did not mention, for an obvious reason, that he more than anyone, the former minister of transport and head of the seaway authority,

is responsible for the Cornwall canal now being on the United States side. I do not think I need to say anything further about that at this time.
Since the last war our country has been confronted with the unprecedented situation that although our production, exports, and incomes have all been increasing, unemployment has also been increasing. This happened after the initial post-war years when everything across Canada was booming and we could sell everything we produced to the war devastated countries of the world before they were able to restore their own industrial establishments. But since then we have had this peculiar situation of increasing production, increasing income and so on, yet at the same time increasing unemployment. This so-called structural unemployment is doubtless partly due to automation, or to what is euphemistically called the rationalization of industry.
I believe that much can be done by the judicious manipulation of tariffs to increase the degree of processing of raw materials for export and to expand secondary industry. Secondary industry, however, is not a complete answer. Howard Smith Paper Mills, in my own home town of Cornwall, has spent some $12 million on a huge new machine which will tremendously increase its production of fine paper, but will not substantially increase employment, although those whc might otherwise be discharged are retaining their jobs.
Nor are massive public works any final solution as they were in the old days of horse-scrapers and wheelbarrows. The former minister of public works, Mr. Winters, once stated that the Canso causeway, which cost $23 million, employed only about 150 men at the height of construction.
The United States writer Galbraith, in a book called "The Affluent Society", contends that increasing automation will produce more consumer goods than we could possibly use. We all want two cars in our garage, but a third car would be more trouble than it is worth. Therefore, he contends, we must concentrate on producing more social capital, such things as more schools, hospitals, libraries, concert halls, parks, conservation, and the elimination of air and water pollution. In other words, we must emphasize those things that make life more liveable. The recent dominion-provincial fiscal conferences should result in more money being made available to the provinces and municipalities for the kind of local public works that will make more jobs and make our towns and cities better places in which to live.

Although the opposition on a previous occasion in this house when this matter was under discussion made about 25 specious suggestions dealing with unemployment, they all boil down to additional training facilities and the appointment of various committees to study the problem. The Senate, as we know, has recently set up a committee under Professor John Deutsch of Queen's University to make exhaustive inquiries into this problem, and we also know, as mentioned by the preceding speaker, that the Prime Minister has set up a royal commission to look into the problem of the automobile industry.
The Minister of Labour has also announced that the federal government, he understands, will pay 75 per cent of the cost of training programs undertaken by any province. Although trades training might assist younger and more mobile cotton workers in Cornwall to find employment elsewhere, I doubt if any industry is prevented from expansion by the absence of skilled help. A determined industry can always hire, train, or import any trained skills required. Mind you, I think the question of vocational training is very important, especially in some areas; but I do not think in itself it will do much to increase the over-all number of jobs available.
Although it is a dull subject which even our grandfathers worried about, I believe that tariff changes are fundamental to increasing employment. Shortly after the last war we had unlimited markets until the war-ravaged countries could reconstruct their industrial establishments. The dilemma which now confronts any federal government is that certain provinces, particularly the central and industrial ones, want the federal government to raise tariffs to protect our automobile, textile and other industries while the rest of Canada wants it to lower tariffs to help sell our raw materials, such as wheat, minerals, timber, and fish. It is the dilemma of conflicting interests in such a diverse and wide country as Canada with many divergent interests and industries. I think it is obvious that we must increase tariffs and quotas against countries like the United States, where we cannot increase our markets, and at the same time decrease them against other countries such as Japan, the British West Indies, perhaps parts of South Africa; in other words, any countries where we can sell more raw materials and more of our other products.
For instance, the United States only purchases from us what she cannot produce at home or buy cheaper elsewhere. That is a fundamental and very obvious fact. Even if we did raise obstacles to the sale of its refrigerators, magazines, et cetera, in Canada,
Supply-Labour
it would not cut the size of the Chicago Tribune in half just to spite Canada, especially when the publishers of this newspaper themselves own one of the largest Canadian paper mills.
I think it is fundamental first of all to appreciate that although we need not fear economic reprisals from the United States, we must realize that whenever it becomes cheaper to substitute southern pine for Canadian spruce in the manufacture of newsprint the United States will have no compunction in doing so. I think the uranium industry knows this only too well.
On the other hand, Japan could utilize all the raw materials that this country could produce, provided that she could sell enough to us to pay for it. The economy of the West Indies federation is complementary to, rather than competitive with, ours and could provide us with a much needed tropic hinterland. If we were really serious about finding markets for our minerals, fish, timber, wheat, et cetera, no Canadian would go to Florida when he could go to Bermuda nor would we buy a single orange from California when they were available from Jamaica
A vast potential market also awaits us in South America's emerging middle classes. Latin Americans are very conscious that Canada is partly a Latin country and the legacy of goodwill towards us created by generations of devoted French Canadian missionaries in those countries should not be neglected.
I believe the answer to our unemployment lies in a drastic revision of our whole tariff structure with whatever changes in GATT and other international commitments may be required. The only alternative, although one which is in contradiction with that idea to some extent, would be to join the European free trade area or some broader Atlantic alliance. If we do neither of these things Canada faces increasing economic integration and eventually political integration with the United States. Certainly the people of Stormont, many of whose ancestors have, like my own, fought the country to our south on three different occasions to preserve Canada's independence, would never consent to our country becoming another Alaska and the greatest objection would doubtless arise from our citizens of French Canadian ancestry who would face not only assimilation but cultural annihilation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member for Stormont will not resent my taking a moment to deal with three of the matters he has raised. I assure him that any intervention I make in connection with the constituency of Stormont is, as I said the other evening, in order to be of assistance to that

Supply-Labour
constituency which I represented in the house for so many years. But I do wish to bring to his attention two or three points in connection with the matter the hon. member raised.
The first is that while it is true that the textile industry has been in difficulties for some years it was the present administration which promised to alter that situation, adverse as it was to the textile industry; it was the Prime Minister who made the statement in Cornwall that he would do away with the dumping of foreign goods which was taking place in the same manner as he had succeeded in dealing with the dumping of agricultural products. There can be no doubt about that. Notwithstanding that statement, the Canada mill, the Dundas mill and Glengarry mill closed down, putting out of work 2,500 people since 1957. I thought I should make that position clear.
The hon. member raised repeatedly the question of the canal being on the United States side of the line and said that this was responsible for the loss of jobs. There is one thing which should never be forgotten and it is that there were three international agreements dealing with the St. Lawrence seaway, the first in 1932 which provided for a canal in Canada and a canal in the United States-the Canadian canal under that agreement was at Crysler island and was, therefore, not in the constituency of Stormont- the second in 1941 when there was an agreement which provided for the two canals being on the United States side of the line and, third, the application which was made in 1952 and which resulted in one canal in Canada at Iroquois and the other canal at Barnhart island opposite Cornwall.
The point I wish to make is this: appreciating and anticipating that position, a plan was prepared by the Department of Transport to look after those people who might be put out of work as a result, and the hon. member has never seen me rise here to contest that plan, because as far as I know the Minister of Transport has put that plan into effect. It has not given jobs to everybody but, to use the words of the Minister of Transport, it has come very close to doing so.
Finally, I wish to say that the position on the Cornwall canal from the point of view of beauty and charm is, as the hon. member for Stormont knows in a horrible condition. I say with deference that were I on the other side of the house I would not permit that situation to continue for one moment because I was the one who as president of the crown corporation promised the people in the Iroquois and Cornwall areas that this condition would not exist, and I would carry out that undertaking. If the member for

Stormont would make representations to the Minister of Transport I am sure he would remedy the terrible situation which now exists along the banks of the Cornwall canal and, in doing so, give the people of that area a great deal more work than they have today.

Perhaps I could ask the hon. gentleman one or two questions with regard to what he just said. Did the former minister of transport contemplate two parallel seaways existing at one and the same time while the traffic pattern had not been formed? We still do not know what the eventual traffic pattern will be in this area. Further, does the former minister think-
