speechtext:
Order. Will the hon.
member please take his seat while the chairman is standing? We are discussing labour items and not the question of where certain canals should go. I recognize the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo.

Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt that unemployment is the most difficult and serious problem facing our country at this time. The fact that there are 80,000 people more out of work this year than were out of work at this time last year indicates that the problem is getting worse. The seriousness of the situation is underlined by the fact that this high degree of unemployment is being experienced at a time of year when job opportunities should be at their peak, when we are enjoying relative prosperity and a stable economy.
In my own province of Newfoundland there are 1,500 more people out of work now than there were last year at this time, and that is a serious handicap to the economy of our province where unemployment in peak periods is as high as one third of the labour force.
Whenever I think about this problem of unemployment I am haunted by the thought that should war break out tomorrow this problem would disappear. In a short space of time money and credit would be made available, our resources would be utilized and even though their labour would be directed into unproductive channels, men would be put to work. Employment would increase and instead of worrying about unemployment we would probably then be worrying about inflation. But war would be only a temporary solution. It would afford only temporary relief and it would be achieved at a tremendous cost of human sacrifice, sorrow and suffering, together with a great destruction of wealth and a vast increase in our burden of debt. With the return of

peace there would be a short period of reconstruction and rebuilding, repairing the devastation, and then again we would be faced with unemployment.
That has been the pattern that has repeated itself over and over again during the past 50 years. Short of war, everyone seems to have his own particular favourite solution to this problem. Organized labour for many years has striven to at least alleviate the unemployment problem by introducing shorter working hours, a shorter work week and by urging retirement at age 65. The present government as its remedy has put forward a program of public works, of winter works projects, of housing construction and of vocational training and education.
Of all the elements in this program education is the only one which makes any permanent contribution. I say that because we know from an analysis of the problem that the greater percentage of the unemployed are people with little education and no skills. I welcome the extension of the program of vocational training which the minister has put forward. I should like to suggest to him that a special provision be made in this program for the training of cooks. There is a shortage of cooks, I believe, all across the country. There is certainly a shortage of them in my own province. We need them for our ships and lumber camps.
As for the other parts of the minister's program, each one of them creates just about as big a problem as it solves. The trouble with public works is that they do not produce any wealth. While they may provide temporary employment they also result in a permanent increase in fixed costs. The same is true of the winter works program. Our chief complaint in that connection relates to the basis on which the federal contribution is made. An analysis of the figures put on the record earlier this year indicates that the largest proportion of federal funds goes to the richer provinces where unemployment is least severe and the poorer provinces which suffer the greatest hardship and the highest proportion of unemployment get the smallest share of these funds. If the minister is going to introduce this program this year I would suggest that a new formula be evolved which would allow these funds to be distributed on the basis of need rather than on a mathematical basis of 50 per cent of shared costs.
The housing program, too, has its disadvantages. It is not good for the housing industry to be turning the housing tap on and off for the purpose of adjusting our unemployment problems. Under those conditions the industry is diverted from its true
Supply-Labour
purpose. When it runs in fits and starts it cannot do adequate planning. In many cases it also results in the construction of houses which remain unsold.
For those of us who subscribe to a free economy it must be evident that there is something wrong with our free enterprise system when we have unemployment of this magnitude. Man was created with certain basic needs of food, clothing and shelter. Free enterprise exists to supply those needs. When we consider that two thirds of the world's population involving hundreds of millions of people lack even the bare necessities of life and many millions of others are in an only slightly better position-there are many hundreds of thousands even in our own country who have only the bare necessities-it will be seen that society must find a solution of this problem.
There is ample scope for our free enterprise system to find employment for the increase in our labour force. The question must naturally arise that if money and credit can be found and made available for the needs of war, why cannot the same thing be done about the needs of peace, which are human needs? I think the answer to that is that private enterprise responds to our demands and our demands are related not to our needs but to our wants.
It must be evident that free enterprise is not really free, because we have needs, we have the surplus manpower and materials required to meet those needs, yet the machine does not go to work to fill those needs. It does not do that because somebody controls the credit which sets the machine in motion, so that the people who control the credit really decide what wants are going to be filled. This is a matter which I think should be inquired into. Until we face this problem honestly I do not think we are ever going to discover the flaws in our free enterprise system which must be corrected if the system is going to function as it was meant to do.
Our socialist friends would solve this problem by changing the system. They would change the free enterprise system to a state controlled enterprise system. In support of that we see countries in the world like Russia and China where no unemployment problem exists. But the unemployment problem has been eliminated by means of work camps and various forms of slave labour such as we hear exist in China. People in these countries have secured employment but only by sacrificing their freedom. None of the remedies tried so far, and which I

Supply-Labour
have just mentioned, has produced a satisfactory solution and in my opinion the reason is that we have not really got down to the basic cause.
Last night the hon. member for Vancouver East suggested that we face facts. I agree with him because I believe there is one fact that we constantly and consistently refuse to face. That fact is that the basic cause of our unemployment is human selfishness. That does not mean that we should start pointing the finger at each other because that statement applies to every single one of us. It is very easy, as some people do, to lay the blame upon the unions. I am not saying that organized labour and its unions are not selfish in some of their demands but they are no more selfish than management.
That is very evident when we note, for example, what happened in the case of steel. Some time ago there was an increase in wages in the steel industry which meant an increase of somewhere around $1.80 per ton in the price of steel. But what happened? The increase in price was not equal to the wage increase. The price of steel went up by about $4 per ton. That kind of selfishness is just as harmful to the economy as is the selfishness of unions.
The difficulty with wage increases is that they result in a sort of struggle between labour and management for a bigger share of profits regardless of what the effects will be upon the consumer who has to buy the product and the economy of the country as a whole. It is this struggle for profit, not profit itself, that is harmful. There is nothing wrong with profits. The only profits that are harmful are those which result from dishonest practices or from wrong motives. But the struggle to claim a share of these profits is resulting in an increase in automation much more rapidly than is good for our country at the present time because it means the disappearance of thousands of jobs which will never exist again.
It is easy to point a finger at some of the labour bosses who exploit the selfishness of the members of their unions but before we point the finger at them let us examine ourselves and see if we are not guilty of something of the same nature in our election promises. The trouble really lies in our basic motives. Free enterprise is not free because it is a slave to materialism. There is plenty in this world for everybody's need but there is not enough for everybody's greed. What is happening at the present time is that we are all engaged in a mad race through an economic jungle where every man is for himself and the devil take the hindmost. We are not dedicated to any great purpose either

nationally or individually. We have nothing bigger to live for or to work for than our own self-interests and that is not big enough for the challenge that faces us today.
We cannot expect to retain our selfishness and reap the fruits of unselfishness. We cannot serve materialism and expect to reap the fruits of the spirit. We cannot have our cake and eat it too. We have tried to do that over and over again and we have got away with it for quite a long time, as the figures which the hon. member for Laurier put on the record a little while ago indicate. We were able to get away with it partly, I think, because we were able to draw on the moral capital which had been built up by our ancestors.
But the situation today is different. Not only is our moral capital beginning to run out but a new factor has entered the picture with the advent of automation, and as a result of that factor there will never again be a situation which will be exactly comparable with the past. Regardless of what the situation may have been in various years in the past, the consequences have now caught up with us and we are faced with a choice. We are faced with the choice that either we must sacrifice our selfishness to our country or we will sacrifice our country to our selfishness.
Unemployment is a tremendous threat to our economy, as the hon. member for Assin-iboia has pointed out. If the problem is not solved there is a very great danger that our economy will collapse completely, and an economic break-down is always the forerunner of ideological penetration. We all know who are waiting and longing for that day to come so they can move in and take over our country. The proposals which have been put forward by labour and by government with respect to changing the system are in fact mere palliatives. They are like aspirin or mustard plasters. They merely deaden the pain; they do not cure the disease. I think we must stop kidding ourselves that a solution can be found in any of these directions because it is really a waste of time. There can be no permanent solution, no real cure, until we come to grips with the basic cause, and that cause lies in the selfish, dishonest and impure motives that govern each one of us. We need a new set of motives because our old ones have failed. Our greatest national need at the present time is moral recovery. Only then will we have the moral clarity to see what changes must be made, what adjustments are required in our industrial machine, what changes must be made in our monetary and credit systems and in our tariff policies. Only then will we have the

moral courage to make the necessary decisions and, to accept whatever sacrifices may be involved. What we need more than anything else at this time in Canada is a great moral purpose, something to which we can dedicate ourselves, individually and as a nation.
Unemployment is mainly a symptom of that deficiency. There is such a purpose. It is to remake the world. The communists are dedicated to this. They are dedicated to the building of a world with a godless materialistic society. But there is a bigger idea than that, and it is to rebuild the world so that we can have a society that will be free from fear, hate and greed. If we are prepared to commit ourselves to that, if we are prepared to make that our national purpose, one of the biggest contributing factors to unemployment will be eliminated. Then empty hands will be filled with work, empty stomachs will be filled with food and empty hearts will be filled with an idea that really satisfies, not only here in Canada but throughout the world.

Mr. Chairman, in dealing with the estimates of the Department of Labour I should like to place before the committee a constructive proposal which would provide a great deal of employment throughout the maritime provinces. While I do not agree that the situation with regard to unemployment is nearly as serious as our friends opposite would indicate, I do feel that if this project were undertaken, perhaps as well as some others, it would serve to minimize some of the present unemployment in the maritimes now and in future years. I refer to the construction of a causeway between Prince Edward Island and the mainland.
I might say that this project has been mooted for a number of years; at least some kind of connection between our province and the mainland by way of a causeway, a tunnel, or even a bridge, has been mooted. The last two named have been deemed to be too expensive in initial cost and maintenance to be practical. It is generally considered that the causeway would be the most suitable. The terms under which Prince Edward Island entered confederation included the assurance of "continuous and efficient communication" with the mainland. This was a specific stipulation in the agreement. We feel at the present time that the causeway is the ideal means by which we can be provided with this efficient and continuous communication with the rest of Canada.
I might say that a great step in this direction was taken when the Borden government provided the ferry service between Borden
Supply-Labour
and Cape Tormentine. Under present day conditions, this service is not good enough. We have three ferries operating in the summertime and they handle the traffic more or less adequately depending on conditions. However, as we all know, there are a great many disadvantages to a ferry service. For one thing, ferries are very expensive operations, and when the haul is short they are always operating at a loss. I know that the present government realizes our problem. As evidence of their good faith, they have given us a survey which, to date, has been very extensive. I might say that the previous government mentioned this project on various occasions. According to a letter received from the Department of Public Works, the former administration spent only $6,000 on a survey whereas, up until the present, this government has spent over $600,000. I feel this is a very good indication of their good faith in trying to decide whether or not this tremendous project is feasible.
This survey is continuing, and I might say that our people are quite satisfied that the government is doing everything it can in that regard. Just the day before yesterday I made a second trip to the national research council to see the model of the causeway set up there and discuss with the engineer in charge some of the problems that are being met. We are hopeful of good results. I should like to impress upon the government again the necessity for the construction of this causeway as a help in avoiding any increase in unemployment in the maritimes.
The causeway itself would be a very economical method of handling the transportation problems existing in that area. The story of causeways or bridges which have replaced ferry services is an interesting one. First of all, they give a very much improved service because they are available for use on a 24-hour basis and, in general, maintenance costs are quite low. This has been proven in the maritime provinces as a result of the construction of the Canso causeway and the Angus L. Macdonald bridge between Dartmouth and Halifax. In fact, I am informed that consideration is being given to the construction of a second bridge in Halifax because traffic has increased so much as a result of the convenience of the bridge. In general, as the graphs show, the revenues from ferry services rise very gradually and steadily, but in the case of the inauguration of causeways or bridges the revenues show an immediate sharp rise. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that such a project would be a very economical one in the long run.
Under the present set-up of the ferry service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland we have one icebreaker which is

Supply-Labour
40 years old, and which will have to be replaced in the very near future. We have a second one which will have to be replaced in about 10 years. And the service really needs a third ferry. If we calculate the cost of a new ferry at approximately $10 million, we get some indication of the high capital outlay required within the next 10 years to maintain this ferry service. In addition, there would have to be extensive dock alterations which would run into several millions of dollars. Also, there are the continuous dredging operations which are required wherever ferry services are operated. The present service is operated by Canadian National Railways, and the deficits incurred are charged up to the Department of Transport. Recently I asked the department for a list of the operating deficits over the past ten years and I should like to place them on Hansard.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I realize that the hon. member was trying to bring out the point that the building of this causeway would help unemployment. However, I think he should relate his remarks to that fact and not to the question of whether or not there have been deficits in the operation of the transportation between the island and the mainland.

I was attempting to develop the subject in order to show the necessity of the project so that hon. members would be acquainted with the need of this project and the consequent employment its construction would provide. I wanted to show the economic feasibility. The engineering feasibility has not yet been decided. However, if it is not proper to continue on that course, I shall abide by your decision, Mr. Chairman.
This project would take possibly six or seven years to build and naturally if you have a large scale project such as this one which is going to take that length of time for its construction it is bound to provided a great deal of work for a great number of people in the area affected. We feel that it would provide much employment for people in the maritimes in the actual construction and in providing the rock and fill necessary and which must be obtained from the mainland. All in all we feel it would have a great effect on the economy of the area. Not only in the construction itself, but in the increased economic activity which would result from the fact that the causeway is there, we feel it would be of great assistance to the general economy of the area in particular, by increasing employment opportunities. I strongly urge that the government proceed with this project if it is deemed to be feasible from an engineering point of view. If this is done,

I am sure that a great deal of work will be provided for a large number of people in the maritime provinces.

In the general discussion so far of the first item in the estimates of the Department of Labour practically all hon. members who have spoken have devoted the major part of their remarks to the subject of unemployment. That fact is understandable because, as has been pointed out by other hon. members, unemployment is our No. 1 domestic problem with the exception, of course, of national security itself. There are a great many other important matters that come within the jurisdiction of my hon. friend and no doubt we shall have an opportunity, when we reach the individual item to bring some of these matters to his attention. Meanwhile, the subject has been unemployment.
Previously, and in this debate, we have criticized the minister and the government for what we consider to be their inadequate action to deal with this problem. If we do that we do not minimize the devoted efforts that have been made by the officials of the department. We do not underestimate the complexity and the difficulty of the problems that confront them and the minister to whose sincerity and devotion in his work we have in the past paid our tribute and are glad to do so today. He presides over a department which, in our complicated industrial society should be, if it is not, one of the most important departments of government. We made this point in the debate last year, and I say this in no political sense, because this matter goes beyond the time of the minister's administration. In the development of our political governmental structure we perhaps have not given the Department of Labour the importance or even perhaps the resources that it should have in order to do the job we ask it to do. That job is becoming more and more important, particularly in this field of employment. When I say that, I do not underestimate its importance in other fields, especially in the field of industrial disputes.
Throughout the present session we on this side of the chamber have warned the government about the unusual and growing level of unemployment in this country. That warning has been repeated today and it was repeated yesterday. We have been pressing for immediate, effective and realistic action in order to deal with this problem. The minister may recall that during the debate on the speech from the throne, I referred to that matter as did some of my colleagues. I dealt with it during the special debate on unemployment which we initiated and again

during the budget debate at the beginning of April. We on this side at that time, and earlier, warned the government against at least the possibility and perhaps the probability of a slow-down. In that warning we ventured to put forward some suggestions that we thought would be helpful but I am bound to say, as has already been said, that our suggestions do not appear to have been taken seriously. We thought they were practical and we thought they were concrete.
Having said that, I should also say that the government now appears to be creeping up on one or two of them. The reaction we obtained to those suggestions at the time- and that reaction has been referred to in this debate-was too often that of jibes and charges-and I am not thinking of the minister particularly in this regard-that we were fomenting an atmosphere of gloom and doom. As my friend the hon. member for Laurier repeated this afternoon, we were told by the Minister of Finance during the budget debate that this unemployment difficulty would disappear with the coming of spring. The Minister of Finance based his optimism apparently and his financial policies reflecting that optimism on the following expectation, and I quote from page 2674 of Hansard. I may say that this was during the budget debate. He said this:
X expect that the forces of expansion will continue during 1960, and that the rates of increase we have experienced in 1959 should be maintained throughout the year.
He stated at that time that he was basing his forecast on an increase in the gross national product in 1960 of about 6 per cent. On this occasion he did not make any allowance for a change in the price level. Those were his predictions and they have an important bearing on this employment situation because if the employment policies or, even more, if the unemployment policies of the government are based on an optimistic prediction, we can begin to understand why nothing effective has been accomplished in that particular field. The facts do not bear out this prediction. I think it was my friend the hon. member for Assiniboia who this afternoon made that apparent by quoting from the dominion bureau of statistics publication National Accounts, Income and Expenditure, first quarter, 1960, page 1. Perhaps I can put the third paragraph on the record again. It reads:
The advance in gross national product moderated in the first quarter of 1960. Apart from the third quarter of last year, the increase of 1 per cent was the smallest quarter to quarter gain in the value of production (seasonally adjusted) since the expansion began following recovery from the 1957-58 recession.
Supply-Labour
That is from the bureau of statistics official publication. We now also have official evidence that in the second quarter of this year economic conditions have not improved materially as compared with last year. There is some evidence of improvement in certain sectors and some evidence of decline in other sectors. These latest bureau of statistics figures are very disturbing to anyone who is worried about this economic position and its effect on employment, because these figures do show that the number of jobs is lagging behind the increase in the work force even though-and members on the government side are continually reminding us of this-the employment figures themselves are up.
In June, 1959 the labour force was 6,287,000. In June, 1960 it was 6,454,000, the highest figure I suppose we have reached. That was an increase from June to June of 167,000. But the significant and not so encouraging feature is that the persons with jobs were
6,053,000	in June, 1959 and 6,154,000 in June, 1960, an increase of only 101,000. In other words, the increase in employment is not keeping pace with the increase in the labour force.
If that is the situation there is bound to be serious unemployment, and all you have to do to get the figures for the unemployed is to deduct the persons with jobs from the figures for the labour force, and you get 300,000 unemployed in June, 1960 as against 234,000 in June, 1959, an increase from June to June of 66,000. In terms of percentages it is an increase from 3.7 per cent in the labour force in June, 1959 to 4.6 per cent in June, 1960. And all this at a time when the increase in the labour force was not as great as it would have been if we had had the kind of immigration we have had in recent years.
If you take the figures for the first six months in 1960, even on the lowest measure of calculation you get 7.5 per cent of the labour force without jobs and seeking work. That is higher than in the corresponding period of 1959 when it was 7.1 per cent. I hope the minister will not accuse me of being unduly pessimistic if I say that in the projection of that trend, unless it is stopped, the average for this year may well be worse than it was in 1959 when it was 5.6 over the year.
On June 30 the jobless claims for unemployment insurance were 35 per cent above last year. These figures are bound to give us cause for concern as we approach mid-summer and will soon be into autumn and winter, and there are other statistics which add to this anxiety. I will anticipate the minister's criticisms. He may say I am picking out a few of the depressing statistics, and I admit they are the ones that worry us. But if

Supply-Labour
you read the current issue of the Financial Post, you will have to admit that there are some indices which are discouraging. The retail trade in May declined by 3.1 per cent. Building permits in the same month were down by 9.3 per cent. Industrial employment in May was below the level for May over the last four years. Railway car loadings, always an important index of general economic activity, in the week ending July 14 were down by 5.4 per cent.
They are some of the indications of the difficulties which are faced by the Canadian economy in the summer of 1960, difficulties which are bound to reflect themselves and are reflecting themselves in terms of unemployment. We say that this situation, signs of which appeared many months ago, requires special action, and needed action many months ago. If the government does not think the kind of action which we are talking about is required, we hope the minister during the course of this debate, or the Minister of Finance when we examine his estimates some time in the future, will give us the information on which he is basing his more optimistic view of the situation.
If we turn to the non-official but qualified economic forecasters we get some even more disturbing predictions. There is a firm in Toronto, a highly regarded firm of economic forecasters, Becket Associates-the minister probably knows them-and their analysis for July, 1960 refers to the "contraction in Canadian business activity continued to widen last month", that is June, and talks about spreading declines in business activities. And this at a time, according to the government, when we are in the midst of full recovery from recession. We are in the midst of expansion and have every reason for economic optimism.
If that is true, what is the situation likely to be if we find ourselves in the months ahead in the midst of a recession? There have been changes in the nature as well as in the volume of employment, and some of these changes in the nature of employment do, I think, have a bearing on our unemployment situation. More women are coming into the labour force and staying in the labour force, which has both social and economic importance. I think the regional character of mu' unemployment difficulties has been accentuated in the last year or two, although we always had it, and I will say something more about that later. Certainly the situation now is worst in those areas where it is most difficult to solve. Furthermore, employment, particularly male employment, is becoming more and more dependent on certain industries, on the service industries, on

the construction industry, and less and less on manufacturing. That also has its significance for government policy.
Mr. Chairman, one out of four of our jobs today still comes from manufacturing in this country; but in 1959 there was 5 per cent fewer jobs in manufacturing than in 1957. This shifting nature of employment can easily be illustrated by a few figures, and I hope the committee will pardon me if I put a few of these figures on the record.
During the decade 1949-59 employment increased in this country by 19 per cent. But construction employment-and by the very nature of it, construction in this country is a seasonal employment to an extent probably not exceeded by any other kind of employment-increased by 30 per cent during that decade. Employment in the services industry increased by 39 per cent, while employment from manufacturing increased only by 11 per cent, which shows that manufacturing is losing its former significance in the economy as a producer of jobs. During the same 10-year period employment in agriculture was down 65 per cent.
Something else should be studied, and that is the nature and extent of our growth generally and whether it is enough to take care of our increasing labour force. If we allow for inflation and the increase in the population the increase in gross national product per capita in constant dollars from 1949 to 1959 was 16 per cent. That is the per capita increase in constant dollars in that decade.
When the hon. member speaks of per capita income in terms of population is he taking into account the fact that during this period the population varied and increased?
It is perfectly true the population increased and so did the gross national product. It works both ways-more people, more income.
And you take it each year?

Yes. From 1956 to 1959 the gross national product per capita in constant dollars has actually gone down 3 per cent. The effect of this on employment must be perfectly obvious. It seems to me to mean that if any recession should come it is likely to be more severe and more difficult to meet in terms of unemployment than the last one, so surely measures similar to those adopted in 1958, such as they were, will be even less effective next time. We should be planning for something else. This does not necessarily mean that a recession is inevitable but certainly we should be planning against that possibility, and we shall not be able to do

this if the problem is not appreciated in parliament in terms of recent developments and unless there is an understanding of its nature and its causes. That is why we on this side of the house say we should be having the kind of examination which would enable the government to cope effectively with the economic difficulties which may be ahead.
In this house.

Yes, in this house by a parliamentary committee. We have already put on record some of the causes of unemployment, and I think my hon. friend from Laurier mentioned some of them this afternoon but it is just as well to remind ourselves that unemployment in this country is not due to any one factor, to any one situation or to any one cause. There is the normal classical cyclical unemployment about which we know a good deal through past experience; an experience which has been so unhappy that it may perhaps hamper the efforts which we should be making to meet the other kinds of unemployment which is other than cyclical.
There is frictional unemployment where people are changing their jobs because there is a declining need for their skills, and moving from one area to another hoping that their skills may be useful in a new area. The minister has indicated that the government is doing something about this problem through retraining programs. We on this side press him to do more in this important field. Perhaps the minister has studied what has been done in Belgium, a country which has made great progress in retraining programs with less by way of resources than we have. Then there is seasonal unemployment which, of course, presents a particular problem to a country such as Canada. In addition, there is technological and structural unemployment. An electric power plant is built and the coal miners find themselves out of a job.
They are not going to be out of a job in New Brunswick.
I hope not.
Mr. Robichaud said so.

When the Canso causeway was built the ferry operators were out of a job, at least for a while. Today we might find 40 men running electronically a huge plant which used to employ 400. That is automation. Today in our economy there is often little relationship in certain industries between the value of a plant's production and the number of men it employs. That certainly has its effects on the employment picture. Then there are international causes. Some of
Supply-Labour
our extractive industries in particular are dependent to a great extent on decisions taken in countries other than our own, although that situation may change as time goes by. We all have examples in the last 12 months in our minds of what can happen in terms of unemployment when another government lets us down as we have been let down by the United States in connection with the uranium industry. Then there are fiscal and economic causes-tight money and that kind of thing.
As hon. members will realize, we cannot solve this problem by any single approach because there is no single cause. No single remedy will do the job.
Economic instability, which causes unemployment, may arise, not only from the basic factors of the economy but also from a particular imbalance in certain regions. It is possible for full employment to be achieved within reasonable limits at a national level while some areas still experience serious unemployment. Our past experience shows that unemployment, when it arises, is always unevenly distributed through the country. Certain regions are more affected than others. This dissimilarity indicates that full employment cannot be ensured simply by a national program applied uniformly throughout the country. If we should try to follow this line of action exclusively a considerable degree of inflation would be reached before an adequate level of employment was achieved in the more depressed areas.
The limitations of a general approach to full employment applied uniformly throughout the country are particularly serious when we consider that our economy is not now and is not likely to be a homogeneous unit. The diversity in the basic factors of Canada's economy and in the conditions of its development have produced very different economic regions with different regional problems. These regions differ in such respects as the composition and the distribution of their population, their natural resources, their industrial structure, their climate and the degree of their economic development.
The actions of these forces produce different types of adaptation to economic change and evolution in our development. Some regions may show signs of decline while others experience a period of growth and development. Given areas may be quite sensitive to short run fluctuations while others remain relatively stable throughout the trade cycle. Different regions are not affected to the same degree by seasonal variations and the direct impact of irregular factors is often local.
Finally, in all these regional reactions there is a time lag which presents special problems.

Supply-Labour
If we combine all those elements we get a great variety of regional behaviours. Perhaps I may be permitted to refer to these elements as divisive elements in the economic sense. When combined we get a great variety of regional behaviours so we will not solve this problem by a single national approach to all these regional problems.
It is well recognized that in certain cor-cumstances a public investment program may be essential to achieve a high and stable level of employment. However, such a program must meet several requirements in order to be effective. It does not seem to me that a public investment program, although it is essential in times of recession, which was put into operation on a national basis without taking into consideration these regional differentiations and difficulties would be successful for the kind of thing we have in mind. As I have just said, we all recognize that in certain circumstances a public investment program may be essential to achieve a high and stable level of employment. I think that (all governments in democratic countries, however capitalistic they may be in their orientation, agree on that. However, in a country like Canada if a program of this type were going to be effective in terms of employment it would have to meet several requirements.
Among those conditions which should be taken into consideration two particular requirements deserve our attention although at first sight they seem evident: we must know when to invest and what is the best kind of investment. A program applied in a haphazard way or one applied evenly throughout the country-even if it were not planned -might involve a tremendous amount of expenditures and yet not be very successful in dealing with the employment problem. If we want to obtain the most effective results with a minimum of expenditure-and that is what we are all after, I suppose especially the Minister of Finance-we must determine the strategic areas of the country where economic fluctuations are first felt and be prepared to act quickly in those areas. Some of those areas spring to mind at once and I do not need to name them.
Moreover, we must also be very careful in selecting the type of investment which is designed to have the most constructive results for the purpose we have in mind. The decision depends primarily on the economic structure of the area where government intervention seems desirable.
All these considerations that I have mentioned to the committee lead, I think, to a very important conclusion. If we want as a nation to deal effectively with the employment problem and at the same time to

minimize the expenditure of public funds we must arrive at a regional formulation of certain national policies, and in order to arrive at such a formulation we must know in greater detail and much more concretely than we do now the different structures and the peculiar behaviour of our economic regions. On this side of the committee we say that if the board on economic development and automation, which we first advocated three years ago and which we still recommend, were to accomplish only that it would render a tremendous service to the country. If the minister can tell us that this is being done by some other source we would like to hear about it.
There are other things, too, that have to be considered carefully. I will only mention them because I do not want to delay the committee. We have to consider the effect of monetary policy on this regional formulation of our problems. I know and the minister knows that at this moment there is a regional approach to monetary policy being investigated in the Atlantic provinces by a royal commission. It would be interesting to know if the Department of Finance has any liaison with that commission.
There is also the question of fiscal incentives on a regional basis for economic development and employment. All of this means planning, planning for the benefit of the individual without depriving him of his initiative, and planning for the development of our country at the same time. I hope I will not be accused of being a socialist if I say that planning for employment is more and more necessary as our economic society becomes more and more complicated, planning with the purpose of giving the individual the opportunity for work, to make life better for him, to give him a better chance for development only if the individual has a better chance for development are we going to have the right kind of national development.
This means for the individual material development, material betterment. I know, and if I did not know I would undoubtedly be reminded, that man cannot live by bread alone; but he must have bread and he must have work by which he can earn that bread. I agree that he should rely primarily on himself to get that bread and even the cake that we like to have to supplement our bread. But the state also has a responsibility to make that possible and the responsibility of the state lies in the creation of sound policies, the creation of an economic climate which will give the individual citizen the best opportunity to look after himself through work under decent conditions and at a fair wage.

The state also has the responsibility of providing by social security legislation a cushion between the citizen and catastrophe, to help him in circumstances where he cannot help himself or support himself. That is why we have pensions, unemployment benefits and such things. They are a recognition of the social responsibility of the state to all its members.
All of this intervention-if you like-by the government, supplements in an essential way but I hope it will only supplement and not replace the primary responsibility of the individual himself and then of his community. This planning is needed now more than ever before especially in terms of unemployment which seems to be facing us now as a problem of almost endemic proportions. It is needed now more than ever before because of this situation and because the state is becoming an increasingly complicated mechanism where the individual is often at the mercy of forces outside his control or indeed, at times, outside his understanding.
Big corporations, big business, big unions, big demands to be protected and assisted, have made big government unavoidable, even big labour departments unavoidable. That is especially true as big, revolutionary changes are taking place. It would be very nice and comforting, as was mentioned by one speaker this afternoon, I think, if we could leave all these things to the free play of economic and social forces inside the state. That is not possible because for one thing the play is no longer free. Of all these responsibilities in planning that I have mentioned, the greatest and perhaps the most difficult-I think the minister will agree with me-is planning by government to keep people at work, planning for full employment and all that means.
I think the effort of the government in this respect has been inadequate. I think greater and more effective planning is needed. I think that planning should be as much social as economic. It has to take into consideration what I have already referred to, the revolution of automation which, as the minister has mentioned, is as important in this decade of the twentieth century as the industrial revolution was in the eighteenth century and almost as difficult for people to understand. We know what happened because of the lack of understanding of the industrial revolution in the eighteenth century. There was unrest, trouble and confusion then, and the forces of democracy and progress were held back because of that fact.
The revolution of automation of the 1960's extends far beyond the problem of jobs although that is an essential part of it, and if
Supply-Labour
labour is to accept this revolution it must be explained to labour. I was glad to hear the minister say something about this in his opening statement. Labour must somehow feel that government and industry can combine with the worker through his trade union to cushion the impact on him of these changes.
Similarly, there is the problem of the older worker, I was going to say something about that but I will save it for another time.
If the government is going to do these things, Mr. Chairman, if it is going to plan for these things, if it is going to make this effort and made it more effectively than we think it has, it would have been a good thing to have had an advisory board of the kind we have mentioned to help the government during the last three years. I think it would have been a good thing also to have had a parliamentary committee working on this problem this session. We tried to get that and, as members know, we were unsuccessful. The other place was more successful. It has set up a committee dealing with this problem, a committee whose work is, I think, commending itself to the government. If that can be done in the other place, would it not have been much better if it could have been done on a joint basis or even done on a House of Commons basis alone?
Is the Leader of the Opposition sure that the members of his party could attend its meetings inasmuch as they have been complaining that there are too many committees?

Oh, yes, we would attend as we are trying to attend all the committees which have been set up in the last few weeks of the session. We first asked that this committee be set up in March. That committee could have been set up in March, 1960. It could have had the same kind of expert staff which the committee of the other place has been fortunate enough to get, and it would have been a good thing if that had been done.
This problem has to be attacked not on one but on many fronts and it certainly should be attacked on the parliamentary front. I repeat that that attack has not been made effectively by the government and that is our main charge against the government in this field.
We have talked a lot about the responsibility for this matter. The responsibility rests on every level of government, municipal, provincial and federal and it rests on every individual too, every trade union leader, every business leader, every member of parliament. But there is a very special responsibility resting on the federal government of our country and the minister himself has accepted this responsibility because when he was talking

Supply-Labour
about this problem on January 22, 1959, he a peasant farmer so I have had some exsaid, as found on page 194 of Hansard:	perience with several aspects of life where
The responsibility in these matters is ours.	at times unemployment has existed.
We ask the government to discharge that responsibility.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I must say that I thoroughly enjoyed the interesting speech by the Leader of the Opposition to which we have just listened. However I should like to bring to the attention of members of the committee that for the first time this afternoon we heard an official denunciation of the classical doctrine of Liberalism which is that the economic forces of the country should be permitted free play. I am delighted to have heard that statement.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member whether he does not realize that the classical definition of Liberalism ended many decades ago?
I do, Mr. Chairman, but it has taken the Leader of the Opposition and his predecessors several decades to admit it publicly in the house.

You are talking about the
nineteenth century.

I wish to bring to the attention of the committee a few ideas recollected in solitude after I woke this morning to milk cows that were not there. I do not have a research staff or the facilities enjoyed by members on the government side, those on the cabinet benches, the Leader of the Opposition and other hon. gentlemen on his side. We have to search for our own information.
You have the Canadian Labour Congress.
Not this member.
May I ask the hon. member whether they have first and second class members in his party?

No. I should explain, Mr. Chairman, that we have specialists in particular subjects. Members of this group deal with certain subjects. However, I wish to have my say regardless of that because I represent the people of Kootenay West.
Don't let them rattle you.

I have had considerable experience in various walks of life which I think permits me to speak on these questions with some degree of objectivity. Many hon. members would not realize it but I have been a member of a trade union for nearly 20 years. I am also a microscopic employer and
Did you say you were a pleasant farmer?

I trust I am, and pleasant in other ways as well. However, before going on with the meat of my address resulting from my research in solitude, I must say that I always listen with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and I could well understand his approach. I listened to him with great interest, particularly to his reference to the moral aspect of the question as far as meeting the problem of unemployment is concerned.
I was interested in his admission that we live in an economic jungle. That is just what democratic socialists have said for years, and it is because we live in an economic jungle under a so-called system of free enterprise that democratic socialists aim to bring some law and order in the economic and social life of that economic jungle. I was very pleased to hear him admit that.
I have said before, and I emphasize again because I think it should be emphasized, that we are faced with a difficult unemployment problem at the present time, for particular reasons.
So far as the world situation is concerned, we are faced with the political dictatorship of communism on the one hand and the economic dictatorship of monopoly capitalism on the other. We, as democratic socialists, believe we have a middle course for remedying this situation through the recognition of democratic principles and the use of free parliamentary institutions. We believe that the state has a responsibility for unemployment and is the only authority that has the power to rescue the casualties of free enterprise and unrestricted monopoly capitalism as it exists today.
Before proceeding to the few other remarks I wish to make, I want to say personally, how delighted I was to listen to the progressive and sensible approach to this problem by the leader of the official opposition. I am sure, first of all, that no thinking person would try to make political capital out of the distress of fellow Canadians or take political advantage of their distress. I am sure that all the members of this committee face this peculiar, and in one sense, modern development in the spirit of working together to find a remedy for the situation. Here we have an abnormal and continuing unemployment which concerns us all and, so far as we are concerned, not only on account of those who are in need but also because of the

great social waste which is involved. Surely we must recognize that it results from the greater increase in our productive capacity as a result of automation than the increase in employment opportunities.
The situation we have at present is, I believe, unique in Canadian history, that is unique in the sense it is a continuing situation during the summer months. Here we have, if my figures are correct and I have only been able to check them hurriedly, the highest total investment in the construction industry this year; we have for early months of this year, the highest total exports from this country. I understand there has been an increase in industrial production, an increase in total employment, an increase in employment income and an increase in corporation profits. Yet while that situation exists we have this unusual paradox of continuing constant unemployment on a large scale.
I am not going to repeat the things that have been mentioned by my colleagues who have dealt with this subject prior to me. I agree with what the leader of the official opposition said when he mentioned that this is a problem that will require co-operation between the federal government and other groups. While, in our opinion, the federal government must give leadership if it is going to solve this problem, we shall require cooperation between the federal and provincial governments, organized labour, organized farm movements and all organized sectors of the community. We believe that that cooperation is essential. However, I am not going to take much of the time of the committee now. We believe that the first thing that is essential is to have a study made of the situation to get the facts with respect to the causes of unemployment, the rate of unemployment and the nature of unemployment. Then we believe it is necessary for this government to accept responsibility for giving leadership in the development of an over-all national plan.
I was particularly interested to hear the leader of the official opposition use the word "planning" quite boldly today. I have heard it used on a few occasions in the past by members of the Liberal party, but rather timidly, in an undertone as it were. I say, for the first time in my experience in this house, the official Leader of the Opposition used the word "planning" boldly and with emphasis. I congratulate him on that account. We believe this planning is the responsibility, in the first instance, of the federal government. Then we believe that as a result of that planning there must be some public agencies or institutions established. This would be the result of the co-operation in
Supply-Labour
the planning, in obtaining all the facts and information, between the federal, provincial and municipal governments and the other bodies I have mentioned. These institutions or agencies must be established so that we can devise an investment policy which will provide for large scale investment in socially desirable projects, self-liquidating projects, if you like, such as the Mica creek dam on the Columbia river, such as schools, hospitals, highways and housing. All of these are socially desirable investments because they are self-liquidating as a result of the profits they return in social services or in revenues to federal or provincial governments.
Then we believe there must be credit provided to financial these socially desirable projects. We recognize, as did the leader of the official opposition, the necessity for careful planning in fiscal policy. I say that if we are going to avoid inflation, credit will have to be used and planning will have to be given effect to, with some measure of control of profits and possibly some control of prices, as a result of negotiations between the various interests concerned. Credit will have to be provided for the carrying on of projects undertaken by the federal government, by the provinces, by municipalities and by cooperative institutions or organizations that undertake projects of this kind at the regional or local level. Then our fiscal policy and our taxation policy will have to be such as to provide tax incentives to private industry and to those wishing to undertake private developments at a time when they will have the greatest impact upon the unemployment situation.
I was very interested in what the leader of the official opposition had to say about diversification. We are all for diversification in planning projects. In my opinion, with complete centralization of power democracy will go out the window. We want diversification, of power and action, and that is why we suggest this planning as a result of cooperation and consultation between various authorities and groups in our society. Then we have to give consideration, as the leader of the official opposition said-I agree with him wholeheartedly-to the national and provincial aspects. There will also have to be regional diversification and some local activity. I also say, Mr. Chairman, that we have not yet really exploited to the full the goodness in people's hearts in local communities or attempted to mobilize this to meet the problem. I know this would not apply to the same extent in the large centres because the problem is much greater, but I know that with some organization and with some co-operation in the smaller centres between labour and management under a plan

Supply-Labour
the problem could be taken care of locally. I am sure of that therefore, I suggest that is the next thing that is required.
In addition to the program I have just mentioned which would provide for those who are now trained and capable of undertaking employment in industry today we must recognize the fact that we have a large number of young people coming out of our schools. In many cases they are not willing to undertake academic studies, they are not concerned with university training since they have not, shall I say, that type of mind, but they would make excellent artisans, technicians and employees of that type.
We are getting short of skilled workers in some trades. From my own experience I know that good bricklayers, and good plumbers are in short supply particularly in the small communities in Canada because there is a tendency for them to go to the larger centres. On that account I think it is necessary for us to undertake a great expansion, first of all in the retraining of adults for other occupations, and that is possible up to a certain age with good effect, and then an increase in our training facilities for the younger people. I mention this matter with some particular knowledge and particular interest because it is one of great concern to the people in the Kootenays and to the people in the interior of British Columbia.
You notice, Mr. Chairman, that I can never make a speech without mentioning the Kootenays. I have always believed in acting as an advertising agent as well as an advocate of the people for the district I represent when I speak in this house. In any event, this is a matter of great interest to the people of the Kootenays because we are without any institutions of this kind and we have increasing numbers of young people coming out of our schools-a good percentage of whom are not going on to high training-who are denied the opportunity to secure this training as artisans, technicians and so on because of the cost involved in going to the large centres.
I suggest that is one aspect of the problem that must be given serious consideration and that any investment in this respect would be a good investment for the future. I believe this retraining is needed to meet the changing requirements of industry and the services in this country and to a certain extent the changing circumstances and requirements of agriculture.
In concluding my few brief remarks may I say this. When that is done I suggest that it is necessary to have an informed public and to have their co-operation. We must inculcate or promote a sense of personal responsibility for meeting the problem of unemployment.
[Mr. Herridge.l
Before taking my seat I want to say that we recognize the concern on the part of the minister with regard to this problem and we recognize that he has done certain things in an effort to remedy the situation but to a very limited extent. Therefore we suggest that much more is required if we are to solve this continuing problem now and in the days ahead.
Finally may I say this. There are two aspects of public policy that require public understanding and co-operation. One is the utilization, development and conservation of human resources and the other is utilization, development and conservation of natural resources. Those two programs require an informed, intelligent and co-operative public. I suggest that the leadership first must come from the federal government in order to secure this understanding and this co-operation in a program designed along the lines I have suggested.
Before the hon. member takes his seat, may I ask him a question?
Yes.

May I ask the hon. gentleman where he has been in the last 15 years? I have in my hand a pamphlet called "Employment and Income", with special reference to the initial period of reconstruction, which was issued by Mr. C. D. Howe when he was minister of reconstruction at the end of the war. I have just been looking through this pamphlet while the hon. member was speaking and I find that the words "plan" "plans" and "planning" occur on practically every page of this blue book, planning which gave this country full employment from 1945 to 1957.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks on the first vote of the estimates of the Department of Labour, although, of course, I reserve the right to put questions when we get to other items of the estimates.
At the outset of my remarks, may I emphasize the fact that, as a result of poor organization of the business of the house, great demands are being made upon us; indeed some of us have had to attend a committee meeting between 6 and 8 p.m.
At all events, as a representative of a riding made up mostly of workers, I feel it is my duty to make a brief review of developments since the beginning of this session with regard to the problem of unemployment which is particularly serious.
The Department of Labour is nothing less than the orphan of the government. It has been the most neglected department, at a time when its problems were certainly heavier than those of the other departments, at least on the domestic front. I do not mean to reflect on the personal qualities of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), nor on his engaging personality, acknowledged by one and all; but the fact remains that his department has been held up to scorn by his colleagues in the cabinet.
So little regard have they had for the Department of Labour that it has been the last concern of the government, and the Minister of Labour, forsaken by his colleagues, helpless in the face of the existing needs in Canada, would have had every reason in the world-and we would have admired him all the more for it-on such a question of principle, to resign from the cabinet which had so badly let him down.
Mr. Chairman, it is very easy, very simple, to go over what has happened since the start of this session. There has been more unemployment than at any time since the thirties. In the speech from the throne, as soon as we arrived in Ottawa, the government failed to attach the necessary importance to the unemployment situation. Indeed the unemployment referred to in the speech was seasonal unemployment. This was first evidence of a lack of vision. As soon as we had arrived, in January, a major problem was being underestimated.
Some time later, during the session, and more particularly during the budget speech

Supply-Labour
on March 31, 1960, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) was passing moratorium or agreement with his creditors, he gave the matter of unemployment just 16 lines in a budget speech that lasted a little over two hours. And if hon. members remember, the only reference made at the time to unemployment, which was then the worst we had had since the thirties, was this statement by the Minister of Finance:
I have confidence, however, that employment will increase as the spring season will give rise to new job opportunities and as economy will keep on expanding.
There has also been legislation involving a winter works program. You will recall that, at the time, the government allowed the opposition to deal with unemployment in general, as well as with the winter works program. We said, at the time, that the winter works program was inadequate, and events proved we were right. Fifty thousand persons at the most, in the whole of Canada, were given temporary employment under that program, while at the time there were about 800,600 unemployed in Canada.
Eight hundred municipalities, at the most, were able to undertake such projects, assuming the largest share of the financial burden when, if I remember well, there are a little over 14,000 municipalities in Canada.
Quite recently the government again announced a winter works program for the coming winter, and again today a restricted program is announced, which will definitely not meet the needs that will be felt next winter.
In other words, the government policy on employment is a resounding failure. However, the opposition has not been chary of advice.
It will be recalled, for instance, that the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) put forward at least ten concrete and serious proposals deserving of consideration.
And if my memory serves me right, on the same evening when those ten proposals were put forward, the Minister of Labour said that opposition members were spending their time making barren criticism, and were not suggesting anything at all. The very next day, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), summarizing the opposition's recommendations and suggestions, offered the government 25 concrete suggestions and proposals which, we believe, would have provided some relief to the unemployed.
I referred just now to the new winter works program. Already, the press in general has expressed the view that this measure

would again be inadequate and, at this point, I would like to read a few words from an editorial of La Presse, of July 28, 1960. I quote:
Since it has been decided to again provide the same type of help, it would seem that we are likely to run into the same problem next winter.
It must further be recognized that this assistance. which is quite a burden on municipalities, is of benefit to only a small minority of the unemployed. Two years ago. it meant jobs for some 30,000 people. Last winter the number rose to 50,000. However, it represents only 2,000,000 working days, or an average of 40 days per worker. And the total of 50,000 did not quite represent 10 per cent of the 560,000 unemployed found in Canada in March 1960.
Mr. Chairman, you will recall that on many occasions we called for a thorough investigation, by the committee on industrial relations, into the whole question of unemployment and employment in Canada. Nothing was done.
Every suggestion we made with regard to unemployment was rejected. And when we consider the events of the past session, we note with amazement that the industrial relations committee is perhaps the only house committee that has not or has hardly met at all during this session. I wonder what explanation can be given in this respect.
Here is a government that likes to boast of having set up standing house committees, of having put members to work; yet the key problem, acknowledged by most Canadians during Gallup polls as being of greatest concern to them, is precisely the one that was not considered by the industrial relations committee.
We did all we could to warn the government. All we could do was to tell the government: here is an urgent problem, one of vital importance to most Canadians. But nothing has been done.
In this regard, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to frighten my hon. friends opposite, nor unnecessarily cause them to lose sleep o'nights, but I wish they would ponder this thought.
Of late, there have been elections in several provinces of this country. There has been, for instance, a provincial election in Quebec. I hope my hon. friends will realize that the major reason for the clean-up that has happened in the province of Quebec was precisely the fact that the former Union Nationale government had stated that unemployment did not concern them. The people of Quebec preferred to entrust the administration of their business to a Liberal government that was

unafraid to say: we shall resolutely carry out our obligations with regard to unemployment.
In the case of New Brunswick, I am fully aware that special emphasis was placed on certain local issues that were thoroughly gone into, such as the hospital insurance question, but I am certainly convinced that if New Brunswick voters showed such concern for matters like the payment of hospitalization insurance premiums, it was first of all, because they were dissatisfied with a government which had not done what was required to fight the unemployment problem.
Under Conservative administration, Mr. Chairman, the Canadian unemployed-and we can say so today when we are about to leave- have been forgotten, abandoned, left high and dry. And in the light of the Prime Minister's famous promise, which, indeed, was the reason why a great number of Conservative members were elected, I say that the jobless have been misled by the government, because after having been elected, this administration refused to stand up to its obligations in the face of unemployment.
May I, Mr. Chairman, ask the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) a question?
You may.

Does the hon. member recall the speech he made on March 15, 1955 as recorded in the French edition of Hansard of that date, page 2175, when he said:
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal members from Quebec are rightly of the opinion that the unemployment problem cannot be settled through speeches.

Mr. Chairman, I did make the comment referred to by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), and 1 repeat it now: the unemployment problem cannot be settled through speeches, nor can it be settled by promises such as the ones you made.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the latest available figures disclose that on June 30, 1960 there were about 300,000 Canadians claiming unemployment insurance benefits.
Therefore, by whatever system we count them, there are 300,000 persons now unemployed and claiming insurance benefits.
If the Minister of Labour had allowed an inquiry into unemployment, he would have learned from his own experts, that about one third of the unemployed registered at our employment offices, have never actually registered because they are not entitled to benefits.

In any case, according to figures coming from unemployment insurance sources,
400,000	Canadian citizens are now reported to be out of work.
I already said it, and I repeat it tonight, those figures represent men with dependents, wives and children, so that in considering this over-all figure of 400,000, we can assume that today, at the end of July 1960, there are at least 700,000 unemployed in Canada, people unable to look after their families, or pay for the medicine they need, people who cannot, like their neighbours or the rest of the population, live a normal life within our economic structure.
Mr. Chairman, I read the statement made by the Minister of Labour when he introduced his estimates. I hope all our unemployed in Canada will read it; however, it would be very interesting to ask young people who have finished their studies in June, what job opportunities are being offered them today.
We could also ask tradesmen about their job opportunities at this time. And I hope I will not be telling the Minister of Labour something he does not already know when I say that, less than a fortnight ago there were a little over 600 plumbers in the city of Montreal who were looking for work and were unable to find any.
The minister referred to a new piece of legislation designed to promote the building industry in Canada. Before he prepares that piece of legislation I hope he will get in touch with his officers in the Montreal area because they will be able to tell him that, at this time, hundreds and thousands of workers in the building trades cannot find any work.
I was quite amused last night when the Minister of Labour asked the hon. member for Hull to mention the name of one unemployed worker in Hull who was looking for a job. I hope the minister's remark will receive all the publicity it deserves, and if so, I would advise him to hire additional secretaries right away, because his office will be flooded with applications within a few days.
On that subject, I should like to renew at this point the appeal I made early in this session to all unemployed, urging them to register as soon as possible at their nearest unemployment insurance office. I think that is a civic duty, because Canada's unemployed, whose number and needs are being denied, have a duty to prove to the federal

Supply-Labour
government that even in the midst of July, we are faced with greater unemployment than in any comparable period in previous years.
Mr. Chairman, there has been reference to responsibility. At this point, I want to pay a tribute to the new premier of the province of Quebec who has recognized that, when it comes to unemployment, all levels of government have a responsibility and that they must try to find a solution. But, since the matter of the government's responsibility in the field of unemployment has been discussed already may I quote again an excerpt from a speech the Minister of Labour made on March 3, 1955 which we find on page 1694 of Hansard:
Neither the municipal nor provincial governments can exert a great deal of control over the causes of unemployment, which are basically economic. The federal government is the only government which under the powers it possesses can exert control over those causes of unemployment.
I feel it is at this time that the municipal and provincial governments should adopt a policy of doing nothing about the present situation in order to force the federal government to take the responsibility which is rightly theirs.
In that respect, Mr. Chairman, now that I have again put on record views expressed by the minister of labour in 1955, to the effect that it is a matter of federal responsibility, we could make a distinction which, I believe, is important. I think that seasonal unemployment is a responsibility to be shared equally by the provinces and of the federal government. There is also technical unemployment due to changes in industry and production methods. I also believe that in this field both the provincial and federal governments share equal responsibility. But in the field of cyclic unemployment, that is unemployment which is the result of monetary restrictions and fiscal problems, there is no doubt that it comes directly under the jurisdiction of the federal government, which has much greater fiscal powers and revenues than the provinces or the municipalities.
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has run out.

Mr. Chairman, I have a suggestion for the Minister of Labour. May I first ask him whether the Department of Labour is considering the possibility of amending the Unemployment Insurance Act in order to make the benefits available to agricultural workers? At present, as they have for years, farmers in this country are having a hard time finding farm labour, in view of the fact
[Mr. Deschatelets.l
that job seekers are not interested in farm jobs because this type of work disqualifies them for unemployment insurance. Therefore I ask the government to consider the feasibility of providing for this, and I should like the minister to state his opinion on that point when he has the floor.

Mr. Chairman, may I add a few words to complete the statement I was making a moment ago. I shall be very brief. I shall only repeat what the Canadian people generally are beginning to think. In other words, what is the opinion today of the average Canadian citizen on this government, particularly in relation to the failure of the means it has taken to solve the unemployment problem.
Mr. Chairman, the Canadian voters, as indicated by a recent Gallup poll, are disillusioned and concerned, because they find that the country is run by visionaries, idealists and dreamers.
In the course of this session, we have discussed all kinds of problems arising out of the imagination of the Prime Minister and his ministers; we have discussed the death penalty, we have discussed the bill of rights.
As for me, just before leaving the House of Commons, I wish to register on behalf of my constituents, people of the working class, their disappointment, their disapproval on the lack of action on the part of this government with regard to one of the most important domestic problems we face today.
Because of this situation, most Canadian voters today want a change in administration as soon as possible. They want a government headed not by dreamers, visionaries or idealists, but by men of action who will take drastic measures, if necessary, and who will fulfil their obligations whenever it is in the interests of Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, the question of unemployment has occupied the house for many hours in the last three sessions of parliament and particularly during the present session. It is my intention this evening, during the few minutes at my disposal, to bring once more to the attention of the minister and the government the present condition of the unemployment insurance fund, but before doing so I should like to place on the record again the statements which have been made in the past by the present Prime Minister, the leader of the government, concerning unemployment. In doing so I wish

to quote his exact words as reported by the press of the country. M'y interpretation of the Prime Minister's remarks will be somewhat different from the interpretation given to the Prime Minister's declarations last evening by the hon. member for Bromo-Mis-sisquoi-I mean Brome-Missisquoi. Judging by his actions in this house on many occasions, I think the hon. member needs a lot of bromo.
Topping the Prime Minister's list of campaign promises was his promise to spend $286 million in the first six months of 1958 to provide works projects for the nation's increasing number of unemployed. As reported in the Winnipeg Free Press of February 3, 1958, the Prime Minister said that his government would not allow the possibility of deficits in the national budget to stand in the way of providing works projects to try to take up the slack in employment.
I would ask the Minister of Labour today, what concrete measures have been introduced since 1958 to take care of the serious condition of unemployment?
