The facts are that on June 22, 1957, the day after the Conservative government took office, the number of persons without jobs and seeking work in this country, as reported by the dominion bureau of statistics, was 162,000. On the same date the number of applicants for employment registered at the national employment office was 266,000. Today, after over three years of Conservative government, the figures at the end of June for persons without jobs and seeking work is over 300,000, while the number of applicants registered for employment is over 400,000.
Again, as reported in the Ottawa Journal of February 15, 1958, the Prime Minister stated on the previous day, February 14, in a speech in his own town of Prince Albert:
"We are defeating the problem," he said. Figures for the last few weeks showed a slower rate of increase in unemployment.
If they were defeating the problem of unemployment at that time, it has been a long and losing fight for the present government. Answering a question which was addressed to him at the time, where did unemployment come from, the Prime Minister had this to say:
In the first place because we tied our economy too closely to the United States, losing our markets everywhere else. Second, because small businessmen were strangled by the tight money policy of the former government.
What did we get from the present government? A few months after assuming office,
Supply-Labour
returning from a trip to the United Kingdom, the Prime Minister made his famous declaration on the diversion of trade; that is about all we got from the government, a speech from the Prime Minister on the diversion of trade. In so far as the tight money policy is concerned, there again we know what conditions were in this country, particularly during 1959. In the same speech in Prince Albert the Prime Minister stated that unemployment was 379,000 in February, 1955, and 308,000 in February, 1956, and this under a Liberal government. It is true that this was under a Liberal administration, but in February, 1958 the number of persons without jobs had risen to 538,000 and in February 1959 it was 559,000. Those registered for jobs at the unemployment office in February, 1959 totalled 798,000 and in February, 1960, 817,000.
Under a Liberal administration, in the month of June, 1955, according to a report given by the Canadian statistical review, the number of people without jobs and seeking work had dropped to 157,000; in June, 1956, it was 117,000; in June, 1957, 162,000. This, Mr. Chairman, was under a Liberal administration. The following year after the Conservatives took office in June, 1958 the number of persons without jobs and seeking work was 370,000; in June, 1959, 234,000; in June, 1960, 300,000. The number of persons registered at the national employment offices is still more revealing. Under a Liberal administration, in June, 1955, they numbered 231,000; in June, 1956, 189,000; in June, 1957, 266,000; but after the Conservative government had taken office the number registered at the national employment office rose in June, 1958, to 506,000; June, 1959, 308,000; and this year, June, 1960, 401,000.
The Prime Minister said:
Did they talk about that then? Did they act?
We have a government today that is not only refusing to talk about unemployment, but a government that is refusing to act and the results are there to show it. On that occasion, the Prime Minister made his famous declaration:
As long as I am Prime Minister, no man or woman is going to suffer from unemployment so long as public works will provide them the assistance they require.
This was at a time when the Prime Minister was speaking about a huge public works program which would total $1,185 million. What has been the result of this

Supply-Labour
program? Is it still in the vision stage or has it turned into a mirage? I have another statement made by the Prime Minister, Mr. Chairman, as reported in the Toronto Star for February 15, 1958:
Canada, he said, was experiencing unemployment because its economy was so tightly tied to that of the United States which also was suffering from an economic decline. No Canadian government could exert influence over the United States economy. But the Liberals were partly to blame for binding Canada's economy so closely to that of the United States.
I ask the Minister of Labour, what change has been made now that we have a Conservative government? Then in a national telecast, as reported in the Montreal Star of February 19,1958, the Prime Minister said:
"As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada," he said in a live telecast, "everything than can be done-everything without regard to limit-will be done to the end that no one will suffer."
It is about time, Mr. Chairman, that the Prime Minister started converting some of his promises into action. Mention has been made in this house on different occasions of the winter works program for which we were asked last year to vote $15 million to cover the share of the federal government. Under present conditions, when our municipalities are overburdened with heavy taxes, at a time when the cost of money is at the highest point in our history, this is no time to call upon our municipalities to go deeper into debt in order to participate in this meagre assistance being offered by the federal government. The federal government offers to pay 50 per cent of the cost of wages, and that barely covers the extra cost of undertaking such projects during the winter months.
I could go on, Mr. Chairman, to repeat many more of the statements made by the Prime Minister concerning unemployment. What this government has done during its three years in office has been to dissipate the $500 million surplus left by the previous administration. They have forced this country into additional debt of over $1| billion. I want to come back, Mr. Chairman, to the position of the unemployment insurance fund. As I said, this administration has dissipated the unemployment insurance fund which was left by the previous administration. In his remarks yesterday the minister said that in the present estimates we would be called upon to vote a sum of $52,000,000, an increase of $13,500,000, to cover the federal contribution to the unemployment insurance fund. This amount will be far from sufficient to save this fund from depletion. When this
[Mr. RobichaudJ
government took office in June of 1957 the unemployment insurance fund was $852 million and according to the latest figures given in this house as reported on page 7019 of Hansard for Wednesday, July 27, as of June 30, of this year the unemployment insurance fund had decreased to $296 million. I would ask the minister whether in this last figure there is included the $10 million lost to the unemployment insurance fund in the last bond transaction.
Under present conditions and notwithstanding the increase in contributions of close to 30 per cent which was forced by this government on the workers of this country effective as of September 1 of last year the fund of the unemployment insurance commission will soon be depleted. I recall that during a committee meeting-I think it was in 1955-the officials of the unemployment insurance commission admitted that at any time the unemployment insurance fund fell below $500 million it would be in a dangerous condition. According to the figures for last year, with less unemployment and with fewer registered for unemployment insurance benefits than we have this year, the unemployment insurance fund from the end of May to the end of November increased by only $42 million. We can foresee that this year, during the present season, notwithstanding this extra contribution, the unemployment insurance fund will be increased by $60 million or $65 million at the most between June 30 and the end of November of this year; and from November on when we shall likely have, owing to lack of policy of the present government, more unemployment than we had last winter, the unemployment insurance fund will be gradually depleted.
I foresee a situation in which at this time next year the fund will be at a figure of approximately $150 million and when there will be in the fund barely sufficient money to cover the operations of the unemployment insurance commission for a further period of six months to eight months. This is therefore the time for the government to take action. This is the time for the minister to advise this house what are the plans of the government toward the unemployment insurance fund. I know that the minister cannot make this committee or the country believe that the fund is not in a serious position. The time has come for action and we expect that before the estimates of the minister are passed by this committee between now and tomorrow the minister will explain to the committee the policy of the government will regard to safeguarding this insurance fund for the labouring class of this country.

Before resuming my seat I would ask the minister this question in view of the statement he made in the presentation of his estimates on May 15 last year to the effect that amendments to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act would be up for discussion during the present session. I would ask the minister to advise the committee now when he expects to bring in the amendments to this act.
Not this session.

The minister told us previously it was not going to be done during this session. We know that it is too late now, although he made the direct statement last year that these amendments would be presented to the house for study during the present session.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall vote 164 carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. Before it is carried, if no one else in the committee wishes to speak, there are one or two things I should like to say because of some of the observations that were made just prior to six o'clock by the hon. member for Kootenay West who appears to have slept, like Rip Van Winkle, if not for 20 years, at least for the past 15 years; or, if not, to have been suffering from temporary amnesia when he was speaking. He suggested that my friend the Leader of the Opposition had taken an entirely new line, had departed from the traditions of the Liberal party in the twentieth century in what he said this afternoon. I think I can show the hon. gentleman very quickly that, far from doing that, what the Leader of the Opposition is doing is following in the footsteps of a leader of the Liberal party who gave a new orientation to this party which had the effect of giving us the kind of full employment we enjoyed in all the years after the war up until the time the present government came into office.
Some hon. Members Oh, oh.

The hon. gentleman suggested that the advocacy of planning-and I do not mean planning in the sense some of the hon. gentleman's friends mean it-and economic planning at that, was something new for the Liberal party. May I say this. In the city of London, on May 30, 1945, in a nation-wide broadcast during the election campaign at that time, Mr. Mackenzie King said this:
The achievement of full employment and social security will require no less careful planning, skilful organization and wise direction than has been needed in achieving a maximum war effort. In peacetime, the planning and direction of government must be exercised in such a way as to increase, and not to decrease, the opportunities for individual freedom and initiative. At the same
Supply-Labour
time, individual freedom and initiative must not be directed to purely selfish ends. These great qualities must be harnessed for the service of humanity. It is the aim of our policies of full employment and social security to reconcile the maximum of individual freedom with the greatest possible measure of mutual aid in the attainment of human welfare.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is the hon. member prepared to identify the ghost writer of that speech?

Mr. Mackenzie King had no need of ghost writers. If the hon. gentleman will go back to the end of a previous war he will And in a volume written by Mr. Mackenzie King many years ago-because I recognize the hon. gentleman's insinuation, I may say-many years before I knew Mr. Mackenzie King and while I was still a school boy, similar sentiments expressed in perhaps somewhat different language because that was prior to the days of broadcasting.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is too modest.

I would suggest that that is the kind of planning for which the Liberal party stood then and for which it stands now.
I should also like to draw to the attention of the hon. gentleman, because of another observation he made, something that Mr. King said in his last broadcast in that same campaign. It was a national broadcast which the hon. member for Carleton will well remember because it was a broadcast that was made in reply to Mr. George McCullagh when at the last moment he was substituted for the hon. gentleman's leader in their last national appeal before the election of 1945. I just recall that interesting bit of history although it is, I confess, somewhat irrelevant to the minister's estimates. But what I would read now is not irrelevant at all; it is completely relevant. This broadcast was delivered from Ottawa and in it Mr. King said this:
The Progressive Conservative party has loudly proclaimed that it is the party of private enterprise, of capitalism; the C.C.F. has equally loudly proclaimed that it is the party of public ownership, of socialism. The Liberal party has never accepted extreme positions. We do not believe that more employment and prosperity will be created by the mere fact of changing the ownership of property from individuals or corporations to the state. Nor do we believe that our free way of life is threatened by the ownership and development by the nation of certain great undertakings. For the Liberal party, the test is what will best serve the general interest, rather than special interests, whether those special interests be the interests of a financial oligarchy or a particular class.
Let me remind you that Liberal governments have been responsible for great national enterprises such as the Canadian National Railways which have served vitally in the defence of freedom in this war; like the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which our Conservative opponents now seem prepared to hand over completely to private

Supply-Labour
interest; like Trans-Canada Air Lines whose opportunity to develop civil aviation in the public interest has been safeguarded by the present government, despite every effort of our Tory opponents to hand this great national development over to private interests.
The Liberal party believes that the largest part of the employment required must be provided by private undertakings, and the present government is taking vigorous steps to encourage private and corporate enterprise; but, we are equally convinced that, in certain fields, the public interest calls for public enterprise in national development. In those fields, we have not, and, in the future, will not hesitate in the general interest to promote bold action by the state.
Lest hon. gentlemen say that that is a statement made before an election, we know what happened afterwards. We know that between 1945 and 1957 there was a condition if not of full employment, in many cases of overfull employment. It is true that in the winter of 1954-55 and 1949-50 there was a recurrence of seasonal unemployment, but there was no summer through that whole period when there was not full employment. And it did not all happen by chance.
It should not be forgotten that at the time Mr. Mackenzie King made those statements and talked about the planning done by that government at that time he was talking about the problem which was right on the edge of being faced by that government and was putting into useful peacetime employment two million men and women who had been in the armed forces or employed in war industry, the most colossal undertaking in the shifting of employment which had taken place up to then in the history of this country. And that was not done by chance; it was done by planning and by Liberal planning.
So I assure the hon. gentleman that if he has awakened from his slumbers or his amnesia is over he will find there has been a great deal of Liberal planning throughout these years.
Mr. Chairman, one only needs to recall some of those things which have been undertaken. One only needs to recall some of the things which over the years we have been responsible for, such as the St. Lawrence seaway, to mention perhaps the most spectacular of them all; at every stage when the economy needed the extra push and stimulus which it received when there were in the government of Canada men of foresight and forethought and planning. Because all the vision in the world is not much use if you have not got the administrative skill and the practical knowledge and the capacity for executive action that is required to turn visions into realities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?
I would be delighted.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Would the hon. member tell the committee where all these supermen have gone now?

Of course, time takes its toll and it is ten years since Mr. Mackenzie King went to his rest; but it will be many, many years before the imprint he made on this country is forgotten. As for Mr. St. Laurent, who succeeded Mr. King and who served this country as prime minister with incomparable skill and administrative capacity, and a capacity to make decisions and get things done and not play politics and play constantly to the gallery, he served this country in the highest office past his seventy fifth birthday, and the last time he asked for the judgment of the people he got more votes than hon. gentlemen opposite.
Oh, oh.

If hon. gentlemen would like me to go on with my biographical catalogue I would be glad to, except that I do not think the Chair would like it because I see the chairman looking rather sternly at me.
Now I want to make a comparison. I have here in my hand the latest blueprint for full employment of the present Prime Minister of Canada. We have not heard much from the Prime Minister about full employment since March. That was in the day when this government still believed that the unemployment would end with the coming of spring. A month later they began to have their doubts and since then they have talked very differently.
What did the Prime Minister say in the broadcast of March 3? I have read these words in the house before and perhaps it will be worth recalling the circumstances when the Prime Minister made this speech. On the evening of March 3, within two hours of the time that a debate on unemployment concluded in this house in which he did not deign to take part, he went on the air and this is what he said:
And as you know, there was the unemployment problem which we inherited.
Two years afterwards the Prime Minister was still talking that nonsense. But we do not hear much more about that today because whatever this government may have inherited in the winter of 1957 and 1958, and the hon. member for Laurier has put figures on the record today which make a mockery of that statement, I do not think even the Prime Minister's colossal gall would be sufficient to persuade the people of this country to believe that that inheritance has

persisted up till now, particularly when we remember that last autumn the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour were all telling us that the recession was over and that everything was rosy in the garden.
If everything was rosy in the garden last October and November it is pretty difficult to blame the not very rosy situation in the summer of I960 on inheritance from the former government. Whatever this government did inherit, if they are any use at all surely in three years they could do something about the situation they inherited, but the plain fact is that hon. gentlemen opposite simply move from one excuse to another. They blamed the Liberal inheritance as long as they could.
What are they trying to do now? They are trying to fob off the whole unemployment problem on the new premier of Quebec. They have to find somebody else to blame all the time. But one cannot get away from the plain fact which was put on the record by my hon. friend from Laurier and underlined so ably by my hon. friend from Gloucester just now. The fact is that the level of unemployment since this government won the election of 1958, when we were told that as long as the present Prime Minister was head of the government no one would suffer in this country through unemployment has been 50 per cent higher and most of the time 100 per cent higher. I am referring to percentages not to absolute figures; if you take absolute figures their record is very much worse. Let me go on a little further with the Prime Minister's program for full employment of March 3, 1960:
As you know, there was an unemployment problem which we inherited. I do not want to see a single day of unnecessary suffering-
"Unnecessary suffering." Hon. members know the comment I made the last time I referred to this, and it is worthy of repetition, particularly as I have been quoting Mr. Mackenzie King this evening. We have gone from "no one will suffer" to "no unnecessary suffering but suffering if necessary". In two years that is the progress which has been made.
"I did not want to see a single day of unnecessary suffering, and neither did my colleagues. The result was that we had to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to provide work from housing and public works and other projects.
If that was the right thing to do in 1958, why is it not the right thing to do in 1960? Why has the government dropped these ideas. Remember that great visionary press release which came out of the east block with all those projects, half of which were, of course, simply in the estimates which had been 79951-0-458
Supply-Labour
prepared by the preceding government and most of the rest of which have not been started? That, I suppose, is the hundreds of millions that were spent. What is happening now?
No money.

But here is what he had the gall to say; here is what the Prime Minister had the colossal impudence to try to tell the Canadian people on March 3. He said: "We planned for a deficit." When you think of what the Prime Minister said in 1957 in that election campaign about how wicked it was to overspend in the way the Liberal government was overspending and how wicked it was to be paying off public debt in the way the Liberal government was paying off that debt, and how he was going to reduce the expenditures of this country by half a billion, how he was going to reduce taxes and still balance the budget, what a change in thinking this represents. Hon. members will recall that promise of a budget made by the Minister of Finance in June, 1957-the one he got ticked off for by the Prime Minister who was over in London because there was a clash in the plans-that was before Mr. Roblin discovered this was a Fleming government and not a Diefenbaker government, and perhaps before the Minister of Finance discovered it, either. Anyway the Prime Minister said they planned for a deficit. Secret plans, probably, or, as my leader says, hidden plans. Perhaps we shall be able to discover it and produce it damatic-ally on some occasion when we get back into power although I do not think the Liberal party will need to resort to histrionics of that kind.
At that stage it will be an antique.

It was an antique when it was produced. The Prime Minister went on to say: "We had to borrow money." Well, that is certainly an understatement. For 12 years, to enable this country to expand, the previous government paid off the debt of this country and made those funds available for the development of this country-and in two years this government put all that debt back. So when they say they had to borrow money they hardly exaggerated, and perhaps the climate they created then may have had a lot to do with the fact that winter is now extended into July. In 1958 winter went into June. It is winter in July now, and seasonal unemployment is an affair of all four seasons.

Supply-Labour
That, of course, is an achievement of this government. The Prime Minister went on to say:
We were, of course, criticized for this, but when I thought of the families of the unemployed I knew for me there was no other course, deficit or no deficit.
What is wrong with that?

What we are entitled to know in a debate on unemployment is whether this is still the policy. Is the blueprint for unemployment now what the Prime Minister said on March 3 or what the Minister of Finance said in the budget, because they are diametrically opposed to each other. The Prime Minister said: "I knew there was no other course for me". Presumably if he knew it then he still knows it today. Presumably this is not something which is entirely in the past. Presumably if it was a good thing to have a deficit in 1958 it is an equally good thing in 1960. But that is not what the Minister of Finance says, although it is what the Prime Minister told the public in a broadcast entitled "The Nation's Business". One cannot blame the people of this country for being confused when this confusion exists right at the top.
Now I come to the Prime Minister's blueprint summed up in one sentence. This is it: "In the same circumstances I would make exactly the same decision again". We have the same circumstances. Where is the decision? What is the decision? What is the government's plan for dealing with unemployment?
I feel sorry for the Minister of Labour. No one can reasonably expect the Minister of Labour to have a plan for dealing with unemployment. As the hon. member for Essex East said earlier in the session, this is not a job for the Minister of Labour, it is a job for the whole government. We should be told by the government, by the head of the government, what the plans are, and those plans should be something much more significant and much more fruitful than the expansion of the winter works program to include a few town halls and the installation of a few street lights. As nearly as I can gather these were the additions which were made to this winter works program in the announcement made the other day before the federal-provincial conference began.
Everybody has said that we desperately need more vocational training in this country, more technical training; that one of our difficulties is that despite the heavy unemployment we have there are still unfilled jobs because we have not competent Canadians in the right places to fill them. What do we find? We find in the estimates

this year that the vote for vocational training has been cut down by over $1 million. It may be that this vote will have to be increased by virtue of the announcement made by the Minister of Labour the other day; I assume that did represent a change which would cost something. But I can say that that was not adequate, either.
What should be done today is what the Mackenzie King government did at the end of the war. At that time we had all these young people coming out of the armed forces many of whom had to go and fight for their country at the time they should have been getting their education. What did the federal government do? It paid for the education of every one of them who wanted it and was capable of taking it.
I do not expect the federal government to provide the vocational schools but they can help provide them. I do not expect the government to run them. The government did not take over the universities or technical schools at the end of the war. I do say, however, that when you have a problem as big as this one and when it has developed to the degree it has in certain provinces that simply have not the provincial revenues to bear themselves all of the burden and that if they do provide the training for these people may find that the people leave the province to secure jobs in another province, it is a national task.
Instead of paying 75 per cent the government should do as the Leader of the Opposition and several other hon. members on this side have suggested over and over again. The government should take over the problem of paying the cost for those persons who are unemployed and who are capable of benefiting from training of such a kind that will make them really employable.
There are a great many other things one could say about this subject but there have been a great many things said already. What I started off to do was to have a small and amicable quarrel with the hon. member for Kootenay West who is one of the most amiable hon. members in this chamber, and I was just led on from one thing to another.
I hope that the Minister of Labour who I think probably agrees with me-although I am not going to test cabinet solidarity by pressing him too far on this point-notwithstanding the fact that this is a Fleming government-will do his best at the treasury board in order to be in a position to do a little better than he is proposing to do about vocational training.
Will the hon. member who is the distinguished archivist and historian of the Liberal party permit a question?
Certainly.
Can the hon. gentleman point to any lines in Hansard which indicate that the Right Hon. Mackenzie King ever spoke about planning in the terms that the Leader of the Opposition did this afternoon?

I do not think I could do that offhand, good though my memory for that kind of thing is. However, given 24 hours notice I think I would have no difficulty in satisfying the hon. member on that point. I would hazard a guess that if the hon. member would look at the debate on the setting up of the department of reconstruction which was done in 1944-there would be many other places to look but that is the most obvious one I can think of-he would find precisely what he is looking for.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure we have all shared to some extent in the enjoyment that has been evident in the chamber in the past few minutes while the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was having a fine time painting word pictures in which he described the Liberal party as having all the wisdom that has existed from the time the world began while we poor people who somehow or other managed to persuade the Canadian people to employ us again were characterized as just a lot of newcomers who go from one stupidity to another.
Oh, I did not say that.

There are very few advantages in growing older but perhaps one is that your memory goes back a little and I should like to bring up one or two points to add to the pleasant picture we have had painted for us by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
The modesty of the hon. member is something that I always respect but when he has added to that additional qualities, when he is speaking not only for himself but for Mr. Mackenzie King and Mr. St. Laurent, then the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate reaches heights to which one can hardly follow at all.
I should like to remind the hon. member of one or two things. According to the hon. member the people of Canada were very fortunate that after world war II we were blessed with a government which did certain things and by its own efforts and wise planning produced for us 15 years of prosperity and after that, sad to relate, when they were defeated and the present government took office, everything began to go wrong.

A very fair description.
79951-0-458J
Supply-Labour

I am glad the Leader of the Opposition thinks I have been fair in describing what was said by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. In refreshing the memory of the hon. member I should like to go back to world war I. Many people have forgotten that there was a first great war, but there actually was, and I should like to recall what happened thereafter. It is important that we remember in our more sober moments that wars have actually taken place. It is good to remember that wars always leave the same situations. They succeed in diverting the working population from the usual things of life to things which we do not use in ordinary times and they leave a tremendous gap to be filled.
That happened in the 1920's. Those who have taken the trouble to learn about the twenties will recall that we had a grand time in that period. We thought we had discovered the secret not only of full employment but of perpetual prosperity, and it went on and on. I do not know if the government of that time took all the credit for it but at any rate we did not hear as much about it.
Because we had unemployment after world war I.

Then after world war II we had a similar situation. There was a world wide shortage and we enjoyed prosperity. I will not say that the government of the day did not help it along. I had a considerable respect for the government of that day although sometimes I succeeded in controlling myself and did not come out and express it. I never said that all the things that that government did were wrong. I am quite sure that I sometimes agreed that it was right. But the picture painted this evening by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate of the government of that period being possessed of all highest wisdom, going from one wise action to another, from victory to delirious victory, is a little more than I can stand.
Then the hon. member brought us to the situation that existed at the beginning of 1957. I think the phrase used was that we "inherited" some unemployment. What was the situation? We had taken over from a government that had been in office for many years. There was some unemployment. I doubt if even the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate would argue that everything was perfect in 1957.
No, nor even in 1956.

I imagine that under pressure the hon. member would say that

Supply-Labour
what we did in 1957 as an immediate palliative in a difficult situation was very good. Then the hon. member brought us to 1958 and 1959.
If the hon. member would permit me to interrupt, I should not like to let that statement pass unchallenged.
Is the hon. member rising to ask me a question or to make a speech? I think I can speak better without the hon. gentleman competing with me.
The hon. member is a spur.

When the hon. member brought us to 1957 I became very interested in his remarks. I often wonder if we do gain in political controversy by refusing utterly to be realistic and by just going all-out and painting extravagant pictures which any, shall I say, fair-minded or independent-minded person, would find very tiresome.
In 1957 we took measures which I think were very effective for the time being. Then in 1958 it looked as if things were very good. We described the situation as best we could and indicated that things were better. We may even sometimes have over-stated it a little. But I would remind the enthusiastic hon. gentleman that we are next door to a nation ten times as big as ours and what was happening here was happening there. I would also say that even though we were disappointed by what happened during 1959 and during the early months of this year, nevertheless the same thing happened in the United States as well. This picture that the hon. gentleman depicted of us as a lot of people who stupidly could not recognize what was going to happen and then suddenly found themselves with a task on their doorstep which they were not fulfilling was to me just the sheerest fantasy, just political enthusiasm running wild.
Let us be perfectly clear about the matter. Statements have been made by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Labour about things that are being done. They are not all being done before the end of next week but they have been indicated and are being done. Much as I respect the speech made this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition, and I did respect it, I do not know that it contained any great new earth-shaking remedies that we have overlooked and which would suddenly set the situation right. As a matter of fact, we know that we live in a world full of difficulties. We are not the only people in difficulty, and so I would ask the hon. gentleman to sleep on this and to come back in the morning and tell us what he really thinks about it all.
Would the hon. member permit me to ask him a question?
Don't make it too hard.

It is a very easy one. The hon. member referred to extravagant language. I wonder what he would think about this sentence in a speech made on March 3, 1960:
When we look at what has been achieved In the short space of time, we can only regret that this policy was not put into effect a good many years ago.
This was the Prime Minister talking about development.

The Prime Minister does not set himself up to be a wizard and to be able to foresee everything that is going to happen. A great many things have already been foreshadowed by the minister. I would also remind the hon. member that with respect to the difficult situation that is developing, which we admit, we are not the only ones who have been taken by surprise to a great extent; the United States and other countries have as well.

Does the minister intend to reply to the various requests that were made, notably the one just made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, for a statement of the government's policy designed to deal with the present unemployment situation?

If the hon. member would take his thoughts back to what I said in my opening statement he would realize that I listed the measures to be taken which were announced within the last week. In addition, I announced another measure to be taken with respect to home improvement loans under which the chartered banks have agreed to make money available for that purpose. I also referred to the closing sentence in the announcement the Prime Minister made last Saturday when he mentioned "other measures" that are now under consideration, and as decisions are arrived at announcements will be made. There is no question of the government sitting idly by and being content to rest on the announcements already made within the last week or so. Rather, other measures are now being considered and as soon as they are ready to be anounced announcements will be made.

Mr. Chairman, I simply want to say that I followed carefully the statement the minister made when he introduced his estimates. I recall the character of his speech. It was largely devoted to a review of the department's general activities. The minister did not say the government had a program under consideration at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Read Hansard and you will see.

The minister
mentioned that the government had announced an acceleration of its housing program. He mentioned that there was going to be further financial assistance of a limited kind for vocational training. He referred to the liberalization to a limited extent of the winter works program. But he surely does not expect the committee to believe that enunciation represents a vigorous program to meet the problem of unemployment which is now serious, which was serious during the winter and serious last autumn. Surely the minister owes the committee a better explanation than the one he has given now and earlier.
I am going to ask the minister whether his department prepares for him an annual forecast some time in the spring or during the year of the unemployment or employment outlook for the coming months. Although we have not learned latterly of the terms, recommendations and analyses of the economic survey or hidden report, we do know that the Department of Trade and Commerce has such a survey made annually. We were told about it by the Prime Minister in the revelations he gave the house regarding this confidential document in 1958. We know that the Bank of Canada prepares a report and undoubtedly the Minister of Finance has such a report prepared for him.
The minister should tell us if there is such a report prepared for him. If there is, should he not table that report, should he not tell us what the employment and unemployment outlook seem to be for this summer, next fall and next winter in the judgment of his officials? We will be called upon shortly to provide moneys for the maintenance and support of a research branch in the Department of Labour, a research branch that is well manned and composed of competent individuals. These gentlemen are engaged for the purpose of assessing the situation. Has such a report been prepared? If there has been, does the minister not think that the house should be informed about its contents? Is there any reason why that report should not be made available? If the Prime Minister thought it was proper to reveal the contents of the economic survey prepared in the Department of Trade and Commerce, surely when we are discussing unemployment we should know from the Minister of Labour whether the kind of prognostications, for instance, made today by the Leader of the Opposition, are valid.
Are these exaggerations? Are these indications of the future sound? If they are sound, then we have a right to ask the minister
Supply-Labour
and the government to outline a program that will be capable of mitigating the severity of unemployment as revealed in these foreshadowings of the future. How can we properly assess the capacity and the validity of the government's program to meet this problem unless we know whether the suggestions as to the future made by hon. members of this party are warranted?
Is there such a report prepared for the minister? If he feels it is a confidential document and that it cannot be given, are we not entitled to have from the minister, if not the actual report, its conclusions, its assessments, its portrayal of the situation? Is the Minister of Labour to be regarded as having satisfied the obligations that are his at the moment unless he gives us at least some general indication of what is contained in such a report, if there is such a report? If the minister says there is no such annual report prepared for him then, of course, that ends it, but I cannot conceive that in the Department of Labour, particularly having in mind the research branch, that that kind of foreshadowing is not given by the departmental officials.
We are entitled to know whether there is such a report, whether it is pessimistic, whether it is optimistic. Does it indicate anything that will confirm the suggestions made by the research organization to which the Leader of the Opposition referred, a body which has indicated that we are going to be confronted with levels of unemployment certainly comparable to what we have had during the past year and the previous year and the previous autumn?
Are these prognostications wrong? They are public. They have been made by these various bodies, and do they confirm the assessment made by my hon. friend's officials? Does the government, if such a report exists, accept the assessment made by these officials, if it has been made? Does the government think they are exaggerated or does the government agree with them? Surely we are entitled to know whether, in the opinion of the government, unemployment is going to be lower or higher in the ensuing period. If we are going to have a high level of unemployment, now in these last days of this session we are entitled to know from the minister what steps the government is now taking; not what steps it is considering taking after the damage has been done, but what steps the government is going to take in anticipation of meeting this problem. Surely that is not an unfair demand to make of the minister.
Then it seems to me we are entitled to know from the minister if these projections into the future are close to the mark, close

Supply-Labour
to the estimate made, and whether the government is going to be prepared to answer the question which I asked the Minister of Labour when I spoke following his statement yesterday, and that is if unemployment is likely in the autumn and next winter to be as serious as last winter. Will the government call parliament together so that these plans and these programs can be considered or is the government going to allow this problem to drag until the next session of parliament is called? This is a proposition that was put to the Prime Minister, and one with which I do not believe he has sought to deal. It is one for which he has the responsibility to deal.
That is nonsense.
My hon. friend says it is nonsense, and I regret he says that.

I say that, if I might interject, because the hon. member has made this charge that I have the responsibility for calling parliament to deal with these matters; that I should make that announcement. The hon. member well knows that if he wishes that information he should inquire of the Prime Minister.

I did not say the
minister was responsible for calling parliament together.
That is exactly what you said, that I should announce parliament will be called.

The minister is a member of the government and he can tell us whether it is the intention of the government, as the result of a collective decision made by cabinet, to call parliament together to deal with this problem if it reaches the serious proportions which have been suggested.
I should like to ask the minister another question. What organization has been set up in cabinet itself to consider this problem? I am not asking the minister to tell us what discussions have taken place in cabinet. This question was put on another occasion and the Prime Minister said that was an improper question, but the Speaker did not agree. It is surely open to us to ask whether the cabinet is organized to deal with this problem. Is there a cabinet committee? Who is the chairman of that committee? Is it the Minister of Labour? Is it the Minister of Finance, or has the chairmanship of that committee been assigned to the Associate Minister of National Defence? Is that the case?
If that is the case, why is it the case? Are we now tying the unemployment problem

to national defence? Is that the policy of the government? Is the Minister of Labour himself a member of that committee? Is the Minister of Finance a member of that committee? These are questions which I feel the Minister of Labour himself must answer if he is to satisfy some of us who are now dealing with this problem.
I do not believe it is possible to satisfy the hon. member for Essex East at all.

My hon. friend says it is not possible to satisfy the member for Essex East. I will say this to the minister. What the minister has said thus far on this problem has certainly not satisfied the member for Essex East. It has satisfied no one in this party, and I am of the opinion it has not satisfied a substantial portion of the Canadian public, because the government in this discussion has sought to underplay and to underestimate the severity of this problem, if we are to judge by the reactions we have had from the minister.
I have one more observation to make. The other day the Prime Minister announced the establishment of a royal commission to examine into the conditions that exist now in the automobile industry. This was pursuant to a request made by the united automobile workers, who made representations to the government a month ago, one week after representations had been made by the management of the various automobile plants in Canada. It followed representations that had been made by the parts manufacturers in that industry. It took the government some time to make the announcement, in spite of the fact that as soon as the representations had been made for the establishment of a royal commission or a reference to the tariff board the Prime Minister intimated his sympathy and support for such a proposition. The Prime Minister thought perhaps the royal commission would be the best vehicle.
Having decided on this course the government should not feel it is discharging its responsibilities as to unemployment in that industry or, for that matter, in allied industries. The government should not feel this device, in itself, is capable of resolving the problem of unemployment generally. The royal commission is a long term project and it is not going to deal with the situation at once. Are we to wait until such a body reports before we have some statement of policy from the government, for instance with regard to the excise tax on automobiles, which the Prime Minister told us during the course of the election campaign would be

removed because of the severity of unemployment. We have had no comment whatever from the minister on this particular subject, notwithstanding the fact it was announced by the Prime Minister as a method of dealing with unemployment in Canada. It is one thing to make an assessment, one thing to make a study of a problem, but these studies take time and they are not to be regarded as vehicles which enable the government to continue its program of procrastination, delay and lack of solutions.
I say these things to the minister. I say that my colleagues regard the minister as an unfortunate prisoner in this situation. We do not blame him personally, but he is the Minister of Labour, and to whom else can we address our remarks if we are not to address them to the minister on these estimates? He is the member of the government who has the responsibility in connection with what the people of Canada regard as the foremost domestic problem, possibly apart from national defence, although the problems there have international tones as well. So, as we get into the estimates that are now going to be discussed, we will be afforded an opportunity of dealing with certain aspects of the problem, but the minister still has an opportunity to rise in his place and examine this problem as it has been examined by the Leader of the Opposition today.
The speech made by the Leader of the Opposition today is one that I know will commend itself to the Minister of Labour. The Minister of Labour will hold it out as a model for all members in opposition, and I will agree with him. The point is that speech made by the Leader of the Opposition is the kind of speech, in part, that should be made by the Minister of Labour. He is the one who should make an analysis; he is the one who should lead in this problem instead of waiting to be prodded into replies, and replies which so far have not revealed that this government has a program consistent with its assurances or which is capable of dealing in a vigorous, fundamental way with a problem that is of great concern to the great majority of the people of our country.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Essex East evidently does not want to accept the statement that has been made by the Prime Minister. As he well knows, being a former privy councillor, no announcements are made until whatever the government wishes to undertake in the way of a particular [DOT] project has been decided on definitely. I cannot make the matter any clearer to him. I doubt greatly whether he will be satisfied with anything at all, knowing him as I do.
Supply-Labour
Then to reiterate the words of the Prime Minister on July 23 as reported in Hansard at page 6817, we find the following:
-and that further projects and plans to meet the unemployment situation will be announced in due course.
The hon. member for Essex East has ridiculed some of the projects that have been put forward. He has called the municipal winter works program a bagatelle.
That is right.
He has said it is not the fulfilment of the recommendations of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities.
Not fully.

I should just like to point out to him that in the submission of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities of April 9, 1959 under the heading of "Unemployment and municipal winter works" this sentence is to be found at page 4:
The municipalities are of the view that the municipal winter works program has justified itself and they commend the dominion government for initiating the program.
I do not quarrel with that statement.

Then again on page 6, in paragraph 4, they say this:
They are also strongly of the view and urge that the range and nature of eligible projects be broadened and extended to include inside as well as outdoor local works, including construction repairs and maintenance on municipal buildings and institutions, water-works and sewerage disposal plants, parks and recreational facilities, maintenance and improvement of municipal sources of water supply and municipal dumps, work on traffic and street name signs, and similar municipal works and requirements.
We have done this in this new broadened program that we have announced, and the hon. member says that is not satisfactory.
That is not sufficient, I said.

That is not sufficient, the hon member says. I have here a letter from the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities dated July 26 over the signature of His Worship Mayor S. L. Buckwold, president. He is the mayor of Saskatoon and president of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities. The letter reads as follows: Dear Mr. Minister,
The widening of the federally-assisted municipal winter works program to include additional types of construction projects which will be eligible for federal financial aid is along the lines of the recommendations made by the federation to the federal government in April, 1958.
The municipal governments will welcome the announcement that federal financial assistance is to be extended to the construction, repairs and maintenance of municipal buildings, as well as

Supply-Labour
outdoor winter construction and maintenance jobs. I am confident that many of them will avail themselves of the enlarged program that will now be possible with a resulting larger volume of local employment during the winter months.
The federal government is to be commended on the action it has taken with respect to this important matter.
Believe me to be
Sincerely yours.
S. L. Buckwold
President.
That letter in itself speaks entirely differently. I refer to the letter of the president of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities. That is contradictory to what was said by the hon. member for Essex East.
He does not say anything different.
The hon. member for Essex East has said things that are not facts and at times there is some question as to the veracity of his statements.

Since my hon. friend has questioned what I have said or in other words has said that what I have said is untrue, let him point out one statement I made that cannot be backed up. What my hon. friend has now said is not different from what I have been saying. I said that this winter works program is a bagatelle, that it does not deal with the problem and the president of this organization does not say that it does.	#

Mr. Chairman, just in order to cite one instance that bears out what I have said with regard to his veracity, here is a statement made by the hon. member. I refer to Hansard, at page 4134, in the second column at the bottom of the page. There we find the following stated by him:
In the Moncton Times of May 17. 1960 at page 14 I find these figures. I presume the editor got his information by calling the local regional office. The number of live claims reported in that area-
These are the exact words.
-for April 30, 1960-
And I want to draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the fact that the hon. member for Essex East says this with regard to the number of live claims reported in that area, that is the maritime area, by the regional office.
-was 714.000, as compared with 610,000 on April 30. 1959.
Then he goes on to say how much it represents. Mr. Chairman, that happens to be the total for all of Canada, not for that area.

It is an obvious misprint.
[Mr. Starr.)
It is an obvious misprint; anybody can see that.
If that is the best the minister can produce, it is not worth much.
Mr. Chairman, no correction has been made of Hansard. It has been taken as a correct statement. He was misleading the house in what he said.
I rise on a point of order-
Mr. Chairman-

-or on a question of privilege. The hon. gentleman has said that he questioned my veracity. That is an unparliamentary statement and I ask the minister to withdraw that statement at once. I am capable of making a mistake but my veracity will stand with that of the hon. gentleman any time.
Mr. Chairman, I want to complete my case.
I have asked the minister to withdraw that statement.
I cannot do so because I have more facts here.
Mr. Chairman-
I was curious, Mr. Chairman-
Mr. Chairman, I have risen on a question of privilege.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Has the minister any comment to make on the point raised by the hon. member for Essex East?
Yes, Mr. Chairman. My comment is that I have further proof that he was trying to mislead the house in the statement that he made.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was referring to the point of order raised by the hon. member for Essex East with regard to the discussion that was going on.

I looked up the Moncton
Times-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the minister will permit me to do so I will indicate to him that of course it is not in accordance with our practice to intimate that an hon. member has not spoken the truth. A difference exists when one says that a statement was not true. That is permitted. However, I would . caution the minister that he was coming close to attributing to the hon. member an intentional misleading of the house, something which is entirely contrary to the rules. He might wish to indicate clearly that such was not his intention.
Mr. Chairman, the point was not that I was misleading the house. The hon. gentleman said that what I said was untrue. He attacked my veracity.

He did not.
Another hon. Member: He did.
The hon. gentleman said that what I had said was a reflection on my veracity. That is what the hon. gentleman has said. I ask him to withdraw that statement, and according to our rules he must do so.
If the hon. member objects to that statement, Mr. Chairman-
I am rising on a point of order.

If the hon. member objects to that statement and if it is your wish that I should withdraw it, Mr. Chairman, I will gladly do so.
I refer again to what was said and I want to repeat it. At the beginning of the paragraph which contains these words "In the Moncton Times of May 17, 1960 I find these figures". I obtained a copy of the Moncton Times dated Tuesday May 17. At page 14 there is an article headed "Spring employment boom seem for Atlantic area". As I look through this whole column or this whole write-up I do not find one figure that was quoted by the hon. member who gave the impression that these figures appeared in the statement in the Moncton Times.
That leads me to believe that I would have-
Would the minister repeat the page reference in Hansard?

It is Hansard for Monday, May 23, 1960, page 4134, the last paragraph in the righthand column.
That naturally leads me to look very closely at some of the statements which are made by the hon. member for Essex East. He wants to know whether there are any reports on the outlooks in the labour department. The hon. member for Essex East was a parliamentary assistant to the minister of labour at one time and knows whether there are any reports or whether there are not. Most certainly there is no need for him to ask for any interdepartmental report which may be in existence, and I do not say there is one, to be revealed to him just because he wants to know. The same thing applies to any matters relating to cabinet decisions. Surely it is not intended that I should break my oath in any way to reveal what is going on in cabinet, in the privy council.
Supply-Labour
No one suggested that.

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend from Essex East brought up some important points and asked some important questions of the minister to which he did not receive a reply. The minister spent most of his time dealing with some statements which the hon. member was supposed to have made in the house last May. If he did make them the minister had an opportunity to deal with them at that time.
What we are doing now is trying to get from the minister an assessment of the position which is facing us in this country at this time in connection with unemployment and what the government is going to do about it. It does not help the unemployed of this country very much to have the minister go back to May and find that the hon. member for Essex East said something which the minister does not like and which my hon. friend will undoubtedly deal with when he gets up.
I ask the minister whether he feels that the assessment we have made of the position is a reasonable one and whether he feels we are facing a difficult and dangerous situation in respect of unemployment. I have a great deal more evidence which I could put on the record, not evidence from our side but evidence which has been submitted by objective experts outside the House of Commons, as to the dangers and difficulties which are facing us in the unemployment situation in this country at the present time.
We are asking the minister whether he feels that there may be trouble ahead next winter, whether he feels that this winter works program which he has mentioned, which he says will be increased, is adequate to deal with the situation which may face us. It is the only program-I think I am fair when I say this-that the minister has put forward in this debate to deal with unemployment. I think the maximum figure under that program last winter that I have seen was some
40,000	jobs.
It was 51,000.

It was 51,000. That was as a result of co-operation between the federal government and the municipalities, at a time when we had hundreds of thousands of unemployed, and these 51,000 jobs were not all created by this particular arrangement. A good many of those jobs would have been in existence through the policies of the municipalities themselves. If we allow that half of those 51,000 jobs were created specifically by the plans of the federal government in co-operation with the municipalities I think we would be fair. That would mean that 26,000 extra jobs were provided

Supply-Labour
lor a few weeks or a month or two to deal with a problem which faced the country in terms of three quarters of a million people at that time out of work.
If the minister says there is to be an increase in that program this year and we may get another 10,000 or 15,000 jobs, does the minister think that will be enough to deal with the situation which confronts or may confront this country in the coming winter?
No, I do not.

If the minister does not think so, perhaps he will indicate to us what other plans the government has in mind.
There is one other question. The hon. member for Essex East made some reference to the organization of the cabinet in respect to unemployment plans. He was not asking for the betrayal of any cabinet secrets. We know the minister cannot be asked to do that and that he would not do it; but we do ask the minister, is there such a thing as a cabinet committee on unemployment which has been working? Surely we are entitled to know that. Surely we are entitled to know if there is cabinet machinery which is specifically dedicated to this particular problem which has been set up by the government, what that machinery is and who is its chairman. Surely that is a fair and reasonable request to make of the minister.

I have found the Leader of the Opposition to be a reasonable man at all times, unlike the hon. member for Essex East. Surely he can understand my position as Minister of Labour, that I can only announce the plans which have been formulated by the government. That is as far as I can go. In relation to the plans which have already been announced, I have quoted the words of the Prime Minister. I hope he can understand that nothing more can be said at this time on these estimates.
With regard to what has been done in the cabinet and whether there is a cabinet committee, the hon. member for Essex East knows that there is, and so does the Leader of the Opposition. They have read it in the papers and the hon. member has quoted the chairman of this committee. What else is there to know? Do they want to know where we meet or what hours we sit?
Who is the chairman?
The same designated member that the hon. member referred to.
Why is not the Minister of Labour the chairman?

The Minister of Labour is an active participant in that committee and there

is no reason why the hon. member should say the Minister of Labour should be chairman. We alternate on many of our cabinet committees, and some of us are chairman on one and some one others.
We have now learned-
You knew it all the time.

-that the rumours we have heard that there is a cabinet committee on unemployment have a foundation in fact. There is such a cabinet committee and the chairman of that cabinet committee is the Associate Minister of National Defence.
If the minister will permit me I propose to deal with one other aspect of this winter works program which I meant to mention a few moments ago but forgot. This is going to be extended in some respects this winter and we hope it will result in some more jobs than those which were created by it last year. But there will be an increasing difficulty this winter, surely the minister admits, because of the fact that some of the municipalities- and my hon. friend who has some experience of municipal administration; he spoke about this last night-will be unable perhaps to take advantage of this program owing to their financial situation.
The submission by the federation of mayors and municipalities to the government of April 9, to which reference has been made more than once, contains this paragraph and I ask the minister to consider this as having a bearing on his new plan for winter works:
By and large, however, it can be said that the financial difficulties that municipal governments are experiencing do not arise primarily from the increased operating and administrative costs of municipal government, nor even from the costs of normal local improvement requirements. The difficulties arise consequent upon the inability of municipal governments to finance the high costs and carrying charges of urban renewal requirements and the requirements occasioned by rapidly expanding urban growth... The difficulties of municipal governments are more in the field of capital costs rather than in the field of actual operating and administrative costs.
Does the minister not think that these figures may prejudice the success of this new and expanded scheme of winter works he has been telling us about?

That may be the case with some municipalities, I have no doubt. I have had experience with municipalities and their problems and I know the difficulties encountered but we are hoping that in the main it will not be so. We hope that interest rates will be lower-they are on the downward trend now -and we hope they will be lower still. However, new municipal work has been going on for years and I feel certain the municipalities will take advantage of this program and that it will be a more satisfactory program

than last year and that many more people will be given employment as a result. That is as far as I am able to know at this time.

We are very interested in this particular aspect of the minister's estimates and I also would like to ask a couple of questions. Possibly they may seem to be in a similar vein but I will endeavour to make them a little more explicit and a little less wordy, perhaps, than the questions asked by the hon. member for Essex East and the Leader of the Opposition.
The minister mentioned with pride that the association of municipalities had expressed appreciation of the winter works program. I should like the minister to say, as the labour spokesman of the government, if the government believes that this winter works program is a cure for this unemployment problem or whether it is just a palliative.

I have said time and time again, and the hon. member must know, that provision for 51,000 jobs is not a cure for unemployment. But we have announced other measures; we have announced the retraining of our unemployed people so that they may fill vacancies that now exist. We have announced an extended home building program; we have got the chartered banks to agree to making home improvement loans. Burther, I want to repeat what the Prime Minister has said, namely that further projects are under study and will be announced as soon as decisions are reached. Certainly the winter works program is not a cure for the whole problem but it should help substantially.

I should like to ask the minister a further question and it is this: has this government given any thought to the problem of the slums, not as a big drive once in a while but as the object of a steady program of slum clearance? The slums grow and grow every day. In view of the unemployment situation has the government given any consideration to a clearance and rehabilitation program which will try to keep up with the growth of the slums on a national scale?

That is a matter which comes under the Department of Public Works. I must say at once that I am not acquainted with all that goes on in that department and its complete undertakings. My understanding is that a number of slum clearance schemes have been entered into with municipalities, but that is all I know.

The Minister of Labour will, I am sure, regret what he said. I have attacked his policies vigorously; I have never attacked him personally as he has done tonight with one hon. member. As I said, we will not forget.
Supply-Labour
It is obvious from an examination of the record what was said on the day to which the minister directed our attention, May 23, 1960. He did not read the whole statement. In the paragraph above I was obviously dealing with the national situation because I said as reported at page 4134:
I was saying that normally we would have had the unemployment statistics for the last available month given to us last Wednesday or Thursday.
Then I went on and said:
The number of live claims reported in that area for April 30, 1960 was 714,000 as compared with
610.000	on April 30, 1959.
Now the population of New Brunswick is about 600,000 including men, women and children, those employed and those unemployed, and how anyone could draw the deduction as the Minister of Labour has done to the effect that I was saying this represented the total number of unemployed in that province is, of course, fantastic. I went on to say:
If that is any indication, then whatever figures may be released later this week or later still, will be an indication that the situation continues to be serious.
It is obvious I was referring to the national figure. For the minister to suggest that I was trying to convey the impression that
714.000	as compared with 610,000 represented the unemployed or the applicants in that province is just too ridiculous to deserve any further mention.

I appreciate the hon. member pointing that out, but when he jumped into that last paragraph he did not start with the first sentence. He started with the second sentence. The first sentence reads as follows:
In the Moncton Times of May 17, 1960 at page 14 I find these figures.
Now there are no figures at all and we find that the figures the hon. member quotes here-he continues-
I presume the editor got his information by calling the local regional office.
Certainly.

I continue:
The number of live claims reported in that area for April 30, 1960 was 714,000 as compared with
610.000	on April 3, 1959.
The record speaks for itself.

May I just say to the minister that I hope he will not continue to make himself ridiculous. Does anyone deny that the local paper could call the local office and get the national figures? Does anyone suggest seriously that the figures for New Brunswick could be anything like that, when those are the national figures? I suggest to the Minister of Labour that by using the kind of argument he does now and as

Supply-Labour
he did a moment ago he reveals a complete bankruptcy of policy with regard to unemployment.
It does not matter what the hon. member says about me personally-

I did not say
anything about you personally.

I am just pointing out what the hon. member put on record in Hansard and led this house to believe. The hon. member had a copy of the Moncton Times on his desk a few minutes ago. He looked it up and did not find those figures and sent the copy away.
That is not a fact. Why does the minister persist in making statements which only reduce his stature.
I do not want to be reduced to the stature of the hon. member for Essex East.
If I was there I would do something about it.

We have come to a sorry state of affairs if members of the house could be deceived by a statement which refers to
703,000	unemployed as applicable to a population as small as that of New Brunswick. If that is misleading hon. members they are, indeed, very easily misled.
But that is not what I got up to say. I wanted to repeat a point which I put to the minister a while ago. I have drawn attention to some of the difficulties and dangers of the unemployment situation which may face us this winter and, in doing so I have tried to avoid what the hon. member for Greenwood rightly deprecated a few moments ago, namely the language of exaggeration. The figures that I gave indicate that there is in our view the likelihood of a situation which may well be as bad as that which prevailed last winter. I ask the minister whether he agrees that that is a reasonable analysis of what might happen in the employment field this winter in the light of the indices which are before us now?
Mr. Chairman, I certainly hope the situation will be much better than it was in the last two winters.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister if he thinks his hopes are as well founded as the hopes he expressed to the Canadian people on "The Nation's Business" on February 4, 1960? I will place the hon. gentleman's words on the record and I think that all hon. members will judge the Minister of Labour by his own words and his own assessment made on February 4 this year over television to the Canadian people with respect to this situation. This is what the hon. gentleman said:

Today, the recession is over and the rate of inflation is at the lowest point in many years, and well below the average rate for the whole century.
The policies we adopted and the measures introduced were effective in beating the recession and in keeping up a level of economic activity that provided more jobs for Canadians than at any time in our history.
Is that not all true?
More and more people to have jobs?
Mr. Chairman, will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes, Mr. Chairman, but perhaps the hon. member should address his question to the author of those words.
I should like to ask the hon. member if he is not referring to the very same minister he expressed the wish to have on his side not too long ago in this chamber?
Well, yes, I think-
Oh, oh.
-I think the hon. gentleman is right and I am not so sure the minister would not be a lot happier if he were on this side.
Certainly you would be. We are talking about your happiness.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman could contain himself, if I may quote the Minister of Justice, and make his speech a little later.
Mr. Pallet!: The great interrupter objects to being interrupted.

No, not very much. I do not think that hon. members can really say I have ever objected very much to being interrupted.
I should like to go on with what the Minister of Labour said in the assessment he gave on February 4, 1960 with respect to the economic situation and the labour picture because these words must be measured. This was a minister of the crown with access to all these secret documents that we are not allowed to see, although hon. gentlemen opposite do not mind exposing the secret documents of other hon. gentlemen, that being their idea of honour. They keep secret their own records but they attempt to distort, take out of context, tear off the covers of documents belonging to other people. A more shocking breach of constitutional practice never took place in the history of this parliament than the Prime Minister perpetrated on January 20, 1958, and there are some of us who will never forget that.
You sure won't.
No, we will never forget that example of the way in which the Prime Minister gets his temporary effects, and for the benefit of hon. gentlemen opposite, I underline the word "temporary".
You have the date wrong. You are all confused.

I go back to the minister's words. The minister was telling the Canadian people about the recession being over, about the rosy world in which we found ourselves in February of 1960. The hon. gentleman went on to say:
There is no defeatist attitude on the part of this government. We will take whatever measures are necessary-
But they will not tell parliament what they are, not even in August. I continue:
-in order that the expansion of our economy will continue and that we will move ever closer to the goal of full employment.
Look at the statistics month by month. There is only one way to describe the way in which we are moving closer to the goal as it has happened since the minister used those words, and that is by reference to Lewis Carroll's "Through the Looking Glass". I continue:
In the meantime, we will continue to take steps to alleviate the situation of those who, through no fault of their own are temporarily unable to establish themselves in the labour market.
I think that latter phrase is gobbledygook for "get a job". I continue:
There was never any room in this country for pessimism. There is less excuse today than ever before.
This was in February, 1960. I continue:
Wherever you look, the outlook is optimistic.
Hear, hear.

The following words are extremely interesting:
More Canadians at work. Labour income on the rise. Exports up. Automobile production setting new records.
It has, too.

I continue:
Canadians spending more and earning more.
That is right.

Note these words:
Certainly in all this, no cause for alarm. There are many problems still to be faced. I would like to assure you of one thing. This government will continue to face up to the problems in the future as it has in the past.
That is exactly of what we are afraid. The government is facing up to the problems of the future exactly as it faced up to problems in the past. How does it face up to them? By turning its back on them and
Supply-Labour
pretending they are not there as it does with this one. The minister went on to say:
We will meet these problems as we met the recession.
You see, it was over by then. I continue: With the help and co-operation of the Canadian people, we will overcome the problems in the same way that the recession has been overcome.
There again, that is just what we are afraid of. We are afraid that the government is meeting this problem now in exactly the same way as it overcame the recession.
