I assume that in making this assessment the minister was speaking honestly. I am not suggesting the contrary. I assume that the minister would not make this statement to the Canadian people without getting the advice of all the advisers of the government because that would have been a pretty dreadful thing to have done if he gave this kind of optimistic report and it was not justified by the advice he received from the economic advisers of the government. If the minister was so misled-so seriously misled -as recently as February of this year, what grounds has the minister for confidence that the hopes he just expressed to my hon. friend without giving any foundation for them-
May I interject now? As a Canadian I have the greatest confidence in the future of this country even though the hon. member seems to lack it.
The hon. member lost his confidence on June 10, 1957.

Mr. Chairman, it is not that I lack confidence in the country. I lack confidence in this government, and I may say that that lack of confidence is shared every day by a growing proportion of the Canadian people. Evidence on every hand has shown this in the last few weeks. But the fact is that I am sure this country will survive this government as it survived the last Tory government. But why, sir, why do we have to suffer these things once in every generation?
Because you are so weak.
That is not a question I expect the minister to answer. That is a question I put to the Canadian people and I am confident how they will answer.
Why not blow that through a pipe line?

The question I do put to the minister, however, is the one put to him by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Essex East. It is a question to which I think the elected representatives of the people are entitled to have a straight and

Supply-Labour
careful answer. That question is this. What is the assessment made by the minister's officials and the other economic advisers of the government who presumably join together to advise this cabinet committee of which we were told-I presume they do not act in the dark-what is their considered joint advice as to the prospects for employment for the coming months and for the coming year?

Mr. Chairman, last night in my argument 1 brought out the fact that on the basis of the 50 per cent that the government gives to municipalities for winter works programs a municipality would gain to the extent of approximately 8.70 per cent by doing a job in the winter instead of the summer. The government pays 50 per cent of the labour cost of any job and the minister told us the other day that labour represented 34 per cent in these jobs. I showed last night that municipalities would benefit to the extent of 8.70 per cent. Municipalities have to pay 5f per cent on their borrowings and very few municipalities are able to borrow money today at 5J per cent or at any cost.
At the end of 1958 the total outstanding debt of all the municipalities of Canada was $3,384,700,000. So far as taxes are concerned, the federal government collects 61.8 per cent of all taxes, the provincial governments 21.3 per cent and the municipalities 16.9 per cent. On the basis of these percentages it is practically impossible for any municipality to undertake any municipal works at the present time unless the federal government comes to its help. How can they undertake winter work programs under the 50 per cent plan when it will only give them an advantage of about 8.70 per cent and they have to borrow money at 5J per cent?

Surely, Mr. Chairman, the minister is going to tell us what in the judgment of the government employment prospects for the next few months are. Maybe the minister cannot tell us what they are going to do about it because they cannot make up their minds. We know that they cannot decide anything, but surely the minister can at least tell us what he considers the problem to be or whether he thinks there is a problem. In February there was no problem, according to the minister, but surely now even the minister realizes, with the kind of figures we had for June, that there is a problem which is not going to fade away by itself. Surely he has enough respect for parliament to tell us what the considered assessment of the government is as to the magnitude of the problem.

Mr. Chairman, I hope there is no question about my respect for parliament. I think it has been above reproach, but that has nothing to do with the question the hon. member asked. I want to say to him, if this is the information he thinks he requires, that I have had no indication from the economics branch as to what the employment picture looks like for the coming fall and winter.
Has the minister asked the economics branch what is their assessment of the future?
In certain discussions with them they have said it is too early to make a prediction yet.
Before the item carries, I see that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has just come into the house and I wonder whether I could ask the minister-
No.

-who is a member of the government and under whose department a very celebrated document is prepared annually, which the minister will well recall, if he can give us a brief summary of the views as to employment prospects that would have been contained in that document.
Carried.
Carried.

The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot says, "Carried". I would expect him, as the representative of a large industrial area, to join with the rest of us in trying to ascertain what are the prospects for employment in this country. The minister has said that the economics and research bureau has said it is too early to indicate what the situation will be in the future, but can the minister tell us what are the prognostications of the economics and research branch as to the situation for the balance of this summer and for the months of September, October and November.
Are you asking me?
Of course I am asking the Minister of Labour.
I have not received any report from that branch on the matter.
Has the minister sought to obtain a report for those months?
No, Mr. Chairman.

Item agreed to.
165. Economics and research branch including research grants and related expenses, $688,895.

Mr. Chairman, this is the vote for the economics and research

branch. Last year the vote was $670,030 and the estimate for this year is $688,895, an increase of $18,865. Will the minister tell us why there is an increase?
Yes. Will the hon. member be patient for a moment until my officials arrive?

While the officials are coming down perhaps I can lay the foundation for the question. The minister said a moment ago that he has not asked the officials of the research branch for an indication of what the unemployment picture is going to be in the future. He has said he has not asked them for an assessment of what the situation is going to be during the balance of this summer and for the months of September, October and November. Yet the Minister of Labour told us earlier tonight that the government was considering plans. How can the government consider plans for the future unless it has some indication of what the employment or unemployment prospects are? Surely the minister does not expect us to believe that there is such incompetence as is revealed in his answer to this question. Surely the Minister of Labour does not wish us to think that he has not ascertained from the research division what is their assessment of the picture in the next few months. If he has not, he has the officials in front of him now, and will they tell him so he can advise the committee before we pass this estimate?
Of the increase of $18,865, $14,000 is for salaries.
New personnel?
No, general increases.
How many people are in the research branch now?
There are 131 plus 5 seasonal.

There are 131 people in the research division of the Department of Labour and yet the minister says he does not know from his conversations with these officials what the prospects for employment are in the next five months. Is that the situation?

I am advised, as I have pointed out, that this is a very difficult situation to assess at this time, and any action taken by the government is being taken on the basis of the present situation and the experience we have had over the past two winters.

Does my hon. friend think that the research officials of his department would find this situation more difficult to assess than the staff of the Bank of Canada, who have surveyed the situation for the foreseeable future? Do the research
Supply-Labour
people in this particular branch disagree with the concern of the Bank of Canada, as stated by the governor in three different cities of this country within the last five months?

I am advised, and this bears out what I have said, that in their opinion this is a very difficult situation to assess. The same situation exists in the United States and to a greater degree at the moment. As a matter of fact, comparing the United States and Canada, 5.5 per cent of the labour force in the United States were unemployed in mid-June whereas in Canada the figure was 4.6 per cent. This is the dilemma with which the economists of the department are faced. There have been times in the past when their forecasts were out a great deal simply because of the difficult and conflicting matters that arose during the time of their assessments.

My hon. friend has said it is a difficult problem. No one has questioned that. What my hon. friend does not hope, I am sure, is to have this committee believe that the research personnel in his department has not made an assessment of the situation for at least the next five months. My hon. friend has said that forecasts can sometimes be proved to be wrong. Of course, that is true. We are not asking whether they are right or wrong, we are asking whether they have made forecasts, and what those forecasts are. What policy is the government devising on the basis of those forecasts?
My hon. friend mentioned the United States. I wish he had gone on and pointed out that they have made forecasts there for the next year. M'y hon. friend might now tell the committee, if he is aware of the committee of the United States Senate, under the chairmanship of Senator Eugene McCarthy, which conducted an inquiry in most of the major cities of the United States with regard to unemployment, and which published a record of its hearings, published its assessment of the problem and its recommendations, for everyone to read. My hon. friend referred to the United States, as though seeking to imply that they have not made an analysis of the future. Let my hon. friend, if he has not got this analysis in his own department, and I can hardly credit that to be the fact, examine the analysis made in the United States. Surely from that, it ought to be possible for him to make a judgment, and having made this judgment determine policies based on it.
I should like to ask the minister how many economists there are in this particular division?

There are 43.

Supply-Labour
Forty three economists and yet my hon. triend wishes to stick to the statement he made that he cannot get from them any forecast for the next five months? Is that the situation?
That is the information with which I am supplied.
I should like to ask-
Carried.

If the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot would like to help the minister get his estimates through I suggest that he stop these ejaculations when an hon. member seeks to get information.
I was going to ask the minister, when I was so politely interrupted, if he thinks it is more difficult for his staff, or for other economists to make forecasts now than it was in 1957?
I do not know why the hon. member refers to 1957. What happened then?
I should like to ask the minister if he thinks it is more difficult now to make forecasts of the employment prospects, more difficult in 1960 than it was in 1957?
I have not checked on that aspect. I did not anticipate a question of that kind.

The reason I ask that
question will be obvious to every hon. member in this committee. In 1958 the Prime Minister took an estimate a year old and blamed the previous government because he said that estimate showed clearly what was going to happen a year later. Of course, as everybody knows, that is utter rubbish, but that is what the Prime Minister said, and that is the grave indictment he made of the former government, that they had hidden the forecast made a year before.
Now the Minister of Labour tells us, practically in August, that it is too early to make a forecast of prospects for next winter. Whom do we believe, this minister or his great leader who said that the Liberal government knew a year ahead what was going to happen in 1958? This is the kind of thing that is destroying the confidence of the people in this administration. I do not believe the minister when he says that his staff has not made such a forecast. I, of course, accept his word if he says they have not given it to him, but I simply do not believe that even this government or the minister would allow a department to employ 43 economists and make no forecast of employment for the next year or the next winter. I just do not believe it at all.
I am afraid the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, will have to accept my word for it.

I do not think I do. I accept the minister's word at once that he does not know; I accept that. But I say I do not believe that his officials have not made such a forecast. I am quite prepared to believe that the minister has not sought to get it, and is not seeking to get it. I do not believe it is hard to guess why, but I just do not believe that this government has as yet made the public service so incompetent and inefficient that this forecast has not been made, because if that is so I do not know what these public servants are being paid to do.
You hired them.

There have been additions, we have been told, to the staff. There have been changes in the staff. As a matter of fact, I think perhaps I made a mistake in not taking issue with whatever hon. gentleman said that we hired them. They were hired by the civil service commission in precisely the same way as public servants are hired now. We had no more to do with hiring them than hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches have now, unless hon. members occupying the treasury benches are behaving in a different way than we did, and I do not believe they are in this particular instance.
I do say we ought to know for what this money is being spent. We ought to know whether this forecast is being made, because after all I was a public servant for a good many years and I was a minister of the crown for some years, so I am not entirely ignorant of how the business of this country is conducted. I know quite well that unless the minister or someone on his behalf or someone on behalf of the Prime Minister has told these officials not to make such a forecast, that such a forecast exists.

The minister has told us the number of economists in the department. He has said that, notwithstanding this display of talent, he has not been able to ascertain from any of their studies, whether or not he can tell the committee what the prospects of employment and unemployment are in the next five months. My hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillingate has asked for a forecast for the next year. I do not dissociate myself from that request, but I am asking for a more limited one. I hope to get from the minister some enlightenment as to his

understanding and appreciation of the situation. I think we are entitled to have this information, and perhaps by further interrogation, we may be able to get some declaration from the minister that will assist us in this matter.
The Minister of Labour heard today the prognostications made by the Leader of the Opposition, on the basis of reports prepared by competent individuals in voluntary and private organizations in this country. My hon. friend has no doubt read the reports of the Bank of Canada. My hon. friend, as a member of the government, surely knows the contents of the economic survey, the hidden report, prepared by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and divulged to this house by the Prime Minister in 1958. What do these reports indicate? Is the minister not in a position, on the basis of that information, if he cannot get it in his own department which I do not credit, to tell us on the basis of these other reports in other departments what is the situation? Is that the situation? I am asking the minister.

I do not know how many times I have to reiterate that I do not intend to go any further than I did originally by saying that there is no report for the next five months. It has not been brought to my attention, and I have been told that it is too early to make any forecast.

My hon. friend has not answered my question. I did not ask him for reports of his department; I ask him to tell us what are the prospects, on the basis of information which he, as a member of the government, has from the Bank of Canada and from the Department of Trade and Commerce. I am asking the minister to give us that information. I am not asking him to table these reports because the government obviously does not want to do that although it did not hesitate to do so when there was a political advantage in so doing. I am asking the minister again to tell us whether, as Minister of Labour in this government, he can give us this information. If he refuses to give it, he warrants the criticism that we level against this government when we assert this government has no policy.
Will the minister deny that reports were prepared in the Department of Labour for the summer months during the years immediately prior to his coming into office? Will the minister say that he does not know that his predecessors were supplied by their economics research division with such reports? If that was the case-and I challenge the minister to deny that it was the case-then did the minister decide to cause that kind
Supply-Labour
of a report or assessment to be discontinued? Does the minister know that such reports existed? If they existed, why were they cut off? This is the only conclusion we can draw from what the minister has just told the committee.

The hon. members know full well that reports come to the minister continually on a seasonal basis or whatever the case may be or however they may be necessary. Those reports were never made public. Those same reports come in to the minister and they are confidential reports. They were never revealed by the former minister who held the same portfolio as I hold nor do I intend to do so.
Until the Prime Minister did it.

We have made progress. The minister has now said that these reports exist but that they are confidential. That is at least something. I asked the minister this very question fully an hour and a half ago, and all that the minister did was to use language which indicated that these reports were not available.
Oh, no.

My hon. friend says no, but that is the situation and Hansard will clearly indicate it. What I am saying to the minister is this. I am not asking him to table these confidential documents. Under the procedures of this house we have no right to have them except there is a strong precedent, based upon the action of the Prime Minister in January of 1958. But now that the minister acknowledges at last that those reports are being prepared by the economics research division, whose vote we are now considering, I ask him to tell us what those reports indicate. What are their prognostications? Do they say that the kind of foreshadowing made today by the Leader of the Opposition is wrong? Are they exaggerated? Is the situation in the next ensuing period a pessimistic or an optimistic one? Surely the minister, now that he acknowledges that these reports exist, and now that we must presume that he has read them, cannot refrain from telling the committee what are the prospects and what are his views as to the situation in the next ensuing period. The minister cannot refuse now on the basis of past policy to give the house this information.
Oh, yes, he can.

This is a free parliament. The information my hon. friend is being asked for is something which the

Supply-Labour
people of Canada have a right to know before we vote this particular estimate.
The only way in which reports can be confidential is if they are kept in confidence. If I revealed them to the hon. member they would not be confidential.

The minister went on a television program last February and he made an optimistic report with regard to employment. Can he tell us whether that report was based on any reports from any economists in his department?
It was a report to the people from a person who has all confidence in the future of the Canadian economy. I always look with a great deal of optimism to the future of this great country.

In other words, what the minister is now saying is that he did not have any basis for that statement except his own optimism. In other words, he went on the program "The Nation's Business" and he made this optimistic statement that the recession was over; that everything was rosy; that they had overcome all the problems or nearly all the problems; and that they would soon overcome the rest of them; and he had no basis for it except his own windy optimism. Is that what he is saying?
Who is windy?

That is the only interpretation that I can put on the minister's words. I am not going to ask the minister whether this particular official or that particular official gave him advice. The question which I asked him and which I repeat is this. Did the minister get a concensus of views from the economic advisers of the government before he went on television and, on his responsibility as a trustee of the people of Canada, told the people that the recession was over, that the outlook was optimistic and that we had no further cause to worry.
Mr. Chairman, I am a member of a government that was elected with an overwhelming majority by the people of this country and I will perform my duties to the best of my ability.

This is a new doctrine, Mr. Chairman. This is a new doctrine from the defenders of the rights of parliament. This is something new. They say, "We obtained a big majority, so the opposition have no right to any information".
Oh, oh.

They say that the people of Canada do not need to be told what the facts are; that they do not need to be told the truth; that the advice of experts and
professionals can be kept hidden from them; although advice a year old, because it was given to another government on a confidential basis, can be betrayed. That is the basis upon which the government operates, according to the minister, in conducting the affairs of this country. For a member of a government that was going to restore the rights of parliament, a government that was going to give to everyone in parliament an equal opportunity; that was going to uphold the rights of the opposition and the rights of the people to know how their affairs were being conducted, it seems to me that this is the most fantastic statement that we have yet heard from this fantastic government. It also seems to me that it is eleven o'clock.
Resolution adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.
May I ask the house leader what the business is for tomorrow?

I greatly appreciate the help of my parliamentary assistant, Mr. Speaker, but perhaps in all the circumstances I should ask the minister about this matter. I think he told us he would throw some light on next week's program this evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We will carry on tomorrow with the estimates. If the Department of Labour is finished we will go on with defence. On Monday the chief legislative item to be considered is third reading of Bill No. C-58, an act to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code. If the committee on the bill of rights reports back to the committee, the bill of rights will be available for discussion on Monday. If there are any other items to be considered on Monday I will advise the house tomorrow.
Did I understand the minister to say that when the Department of Labour was completed tomorrow we would begin with finance?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No; defence.
I am sorry but I did not hear the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: If I said finance, what I intended to say was defence.
There is no doubt about it; it is defence?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, there is no doubt. The order is the same.
I wish to thank the minister.

It being two minutes after eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to special order.
